docs.title: About the A-LIFE RDM Documentation Collection
docs.text:
The A-LIFE RDM Documentation Collection is a collaborative initiative by Brett Olivier and Irene Martorelli. The goal of this collection is to support A-LIFE researchers and make their research data management journey as smooth and enjoyable as possible.

We are only human and always open to improvement, so please get in touch if you spot any incorrect information or broken links, or if you would like us to add guides on a specific tool or method that is not yet covered.

docs.title: How we can help
docs.text:
We are very happy to help! Things we can support you with:

  • Organising, managing or transferring your data
  • Finding the right tools and storage solutions for your data
  • Directing you to the right expert for research data support
  • Finding solutions to make your data more visible and reusable
  • Resolving any issues you encounter along the way
  • Getting you through the less glamorous stages of the data life cycle

docs.title: How can I start using Yoda?
docs.text: To use Yoda, you need to request access to a Yoda Research Storage Space. Please follow the workflow steps described in Step 1 — Getting Started of the Yoda documentation.

docs.title: How do I add an external user?
docs.text: Follow the guidance in Step 4 — Manage Group Members of the Yoda documentation.

docs.title: What do I need to do to archive data in Yoda?
docs.text: Please follow the instructions in Step 6 — Archiving Data of the Yoda documentation.

docs.title: How can I publish in Yoda?
docs.text: By publishing in Yoda, you will get a DOI that resolves to your dataset. Please follow the instructions in Step 7 — Publishing Data of the Yoda documentation.

docs.title: How can I start using Research Drive?
docs.text: To use Research Drive, you need to fill in the Request Storage Space form to get access. Once submitted, follow the steps in Step 1 — Getting Started of the Research Drive documentation.

docs.title: How can I archive data sitting in Research Drive?
docs.text: Research Drive is designed for active storage only — data stored here is not preserved for the long term, does not receive a DOI, and cannot be published directly. Once your project is complete, you need to move your data to a dedicated archiving and publishing platform. See Step 5 — Archiving and Publishing your Data in the Research Drive documentation.

docs.title: How do I log in to Zenodo?
docs.text: You can log in to Zenodo using your institutional account via ORCID or GitHub. Please follow the steps in Getting Started with Zenodo for more information.

docs.title: Does Zenodo need a README file?
docs.text:
Good question! Adding a README file is not a requirement, but we strongly recommend it. Communities, reviewers, and anyone who reaches your dataset will expect to find one — it is the first thing people look for when exploring a data publication.

Please follow the instructions in README — Zenodo Documentation to add one to your package.

Set your README as a preview file

It is highly recommended to select the README.md as a preview file in Zenodo. This makes it the first thing visible when someone opens your dataset — serving as a cover for your publication. See Select your preview file in the Zenodo Getting Started documentation.

docs.title: Licences
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Licences page, part of Essentials in the A-LIFE RDM GEMs collection.

This page provides a reference overview of the most common open data licences used in research data management, including custom licence options for restricted or closed datasets at VU Amsterdam.

Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-06-24 — Version: 0.2.0

docs.title: What is a licence?
docs.text: A licence defines how others may use, share, and build upon your data. Choosing the right licence is an important step when archiving or publishing a dataset — it determines who can access your data and under what conditions.

docs.title: Common Open Licences for VU research data
docs.text:
Recommendation for A-LIFE researchers

For most research data at A-LIFE intended for public access, an open licence such as CC BY 4.0 is recommended. This allows others to reuse your data freely as long as they give you credit.

Licence Source Description Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 CC BY 4.0 Allows reuse with attribution — recommended for most research data Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 CC BY-SA 4.0 Reuse with attribution; derivatives must use the same licence Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 Non-commercial use only Creative Commons Zero v1.0 Universal CC0 1.0 No copyright reserved — public domain Open Data Commons Attribution License v1.0 ODC-BY Open sharing with attribution

docs.title: Custom Licences for VU research data
docs.text:
When data is Restricted (available upon request) or Closed (not publicly accessible), a standard open licence cannot be applied. In these cases, VU Amsterdam provides custom licence templates that must be added manually to the data package as a license.txt file.

For guidance on selecting the appropriate licence for your dataset, see the VU RDM documentation — Selecting a licence for your dataset.

Licence Template Description VU Restricted Licence Download template For datasets available upon request — requires contact person details VU Closed Licence Download template For datasets not made available — only metadata is visible

Custom licence in Yoda

In the Yoda Metadata Form, selecting Restricted or Closed in Data Package Access automatically limits the License field to Custom only. You must upload the appropriate license.txt file manually to the data package folder.

docs.title: GitHub and software repository licences
docs.text:
Licences for software and code repositories follow different conventions than data licences. GitHub provides a built-in licence selector when creating a repository, and uses the American English spelling License in its interface and file naming (LICENSE).

Resource Description Licensing a repository GitHub documentation on adding a licence to a repository GitHub licence templates Collection of standard licence templates used in GitHub How to add a licence to GitHub Step-by-step guide for adding a licence file to a GitHub repository Plain Language Licence Summaries Explains what each licence allows, forbids, and requires in simple terms

docs.title: Tools to help you select an appropriate licence
docs.text: Tool Description Choose a License Simple guide to picking the right licence for your project CC License Chooser Interactive tool to select the right Creative Commons licence License Selector (UFAL) Questionnaire-based tool to help choose a licence — also used at VU

docs.title: Further reading

docs.title: Licence or License?
docs.text:
Both spellings are correct — Licence is the British English spelling, while License is the American English spelling. In practice, you will encounter both in documentation and on websites, sometimes even within the same platform.

Spelling in this documentation

This documentation uses Licence throughout. However, some of the resources and sources we refer to — including tools such as GitHub and Yoda, and pages on the VU RDM website (rdm.vu.nl) — use License or both spellings interchangeably. Both are valid and refer to the same thing.

docs.title: Persistent Identifiers (PIDs)
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Persistent Identifiers page, part of Essentials in the A-LIFE RDM GEMs collection.

This page introduces Persistent Identifiers (PIDs) used in research — what they are, why they matter, and how to use them as an A-LIFE researcher.

  • What are PIDs?
  • DOI — Digital Object Identifier
  • ORCID — Researcher Identifier
  • ROR — Research Organisation Identifier

Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-06-24 — Version: 0.1.0

docs.title: What are PIDs?
docs.text:
A Persistent Identifier (PID) is a long-lasting reference to a digital resource — such as a dataset, a researcher, or an organisation. Unlike regular URLs, PIDs are designed to remain stable even if the underlying resource moves or changes location.

PIDs play a central role in making research Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable — the FAIR principles. They help connect research outputs, researchers, and organisations in a reliable and unambiguous way.

Why use PIDs?

  • Ensure your work remains findable and citable over time
  • Prevent ambiguity — uniquely identify people, organisations, and outputs
  • Enable cross-platform connections between datasets, publications, and researchers
  • Save time — enter your information once and reuse it across platforms

docs.title: Types of PIDs
docs.text: PID Identifies Used for DOI A digital object (dataset, publication) Citing and finding research outputs ORCID A researcher Connecting research outputs to their author ROR A research organisation Linking datasets and publications to an institution

docs.title: DOI — Digital Object Identifier
docs.text:
A DOI (Digital Object Identifier) is a persistent link assigned to a digital resource — most commonly a publication or dataset — that remains stable regardless of where the resource is hosted.

When you publish your dataset through an archiving platform, a DOI is automatically assigned to your data package. The DOI provides a permanent landing page containing your dataset's metadata and access information.

Platforms that assign DOIs to research data at VU:

  • Yoda — DOI is assigned when a data package is approved for publication in the Vault
  • Zenodo — DOI is assigned upon uploading and publishing a dataset

VU Yoda published datasets

Browse datasets published through VU Yoda via DataCite Commons.

What is DataCite?

DataCite is the organisation that registers DOIs for research data. When your dataset is published in Yoda or Zenodo, its metadata is registered with DataCite and becomes searchable in their catalogue.

docs.title: ORCID — Researcher Identifier
docs.text:
ORCID (Open Researcher and Contributor ID) is a free, persistent identifier for researchers. It provides a unique ID that distinguishes you from other researchers — even those with the same name — and connects your research outputs, affiliations, and funding records across platforms.

Recommendation for A-LIFE researchers

It is highly recommended to create and maintain an ORCID. It is free, takes minutes to set up, and makes your research more visible and your contributions more accurately credited.

Register for an ORCID

Why ORCID matters:

  • Prevents name ambiguity — your ORCID is unique to you, regardless of name changes or common names
  • Enhances discoverability — your publications, datasets, and affiliations are linked under a single record
  • Saves time — enter your information once and reuse it across funding applications, journal submissions, and platforms
  • Connects your work — ORCID integrates with many platforms used in research

Where ORCID is used at A-LIFE:

Platform How ORCID is used Yoda Recommended as Person Identifier for Creators and Contributors in the Yoda Metadata Form Zenodo Can be linked to your Zenodo account for automatic author recognition GitHub Can be added to your profile and CITATION.cff files to credit contributors Pure (VU) Used to connect your VU research output record to your ORCID Funding applications Many funders (e.g. NWO, ERC) require or recommend ORCID

Adding ORCID to your Yoda metadata

When completing the Yoda Metadata Form, you can add your ORCID as a Person Identifier for each Creator and Contributor. Use the full HTTPS URL format: https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000. See BP — Yoda — Metadata Form for details.

docs.title: ROR — Research Organisation Identifier
docs.text:
ROR (Research Organization Registry) is a global, community-led registry of persistent identifiers for research organisations. It provides a unique ID for each institution, enabling accurate and unambiguous affiliation metadata across platforms and publications.

ROR is increasingly used in metadata forms, funding systems, and publishing workflows to standardise how organisations are identified and linked.

VU Amsterdam ROR:

VU Amsterdam — ROR Identifier

The official ROR for Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam is:

https://ror.org/008xxew50 — Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

Use this identifier when selecting your affiliation in the Yoda Metadata Form, Zenodo, or any other platform that requests a ROR.

A-LIFE is not yet listed in ROR

As of the last record update (2025-05-20), A-LIFE (Amsterdam Institute for Life and Environment) does not yet have its own entry in the ROR registry. When asked for your affiliation ROR, use the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam ROR identifier above.

If you would like A-LIFE to be added to ROR, organisations can be suggested via the ROR request process.

docs.title: README
docs.text:
Overview

This is the README page, part of Essentials in the A-LIFE RDM GEMs collection.

This page explains what a README file is, why it matters, and provides a template and guidance to get started:

  • What is a README?
  • Why include a README?
  • Best Practices for a Good README File
  • What to Include in a README
  • README Template — Get Inspired
  • Examples from A-LIFE Researchers

Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-06-27 — Version: 0.2.0

docs.title: What is a README?
docs.text:
A README is a plain text file (.md or .txt) included with your dataset that describes its content. It is the first thing someone should read when they access your data — think of it as the cover page and table of contents for your dataset.

A README is not a Yoda or Zenodo-specific requirement: it is a universal best practice that applies to any folder or data package, regardless of where it is stored. A README written during your active project in Research Drive can be transferred directly into Yoda or Zenodo without modification when you archive your data.

docs.title: Why include a README?
docs.text:
• Makes your dataset understandable to others — and to your future self
  • Required or strongly recommended by most repositories (Zenodo, Yoda)
  • Supports the FAIR principles — Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable
  • Reduces the number of questions you receive from people trying to reuse your data
  • Ensures continuity when collaborators change or projects are revisited years later

docs.title: Best Practices for a Good README File
docs.text:
The following best practices are adapted from the Cornell Data Services README guide — our top recommendation for writing READMEs for research data.

  • Write in plain text — use .md or .txt format; avoid proprietary formats like Word
  • One README per logical cluster of files — a single README can cover multiple related files; create separate READMEs for unrelated datasets
  • Name it clearly — use README.md or README.txt so it is immediately visible and recognisable
  • Place it at the root of the data package folder so it is the first file anyone sees
  • Use standardised date formats — YYYY-MM-DD (ISO 8601) throughout
  • Be consistent — if you have multiple READMEs across a project, use the same structure and terminology in each

docs.title: What to Include in a README
docs.text:
Highly recommended

Cornell Data Services — Writing READMEs for Research Data — the most complete and practical README guide available, with a downloadable template adapted for research data reuse. We strongly recommend bookmarking this page.

The sections below follow the structure recommended by Cornell Data Services1. Fields in bold are the minimum recommended for data reuse.

General information

  • Dataset title
  • Authors — names, affiliations, ORCID identifiers; include principal investigator and contact person
  • Date of data collection — single date or range in YYYY-MM-DD format
  • Geographic location of data collection (if applicable)
  • Funding sources

Data and file overview

  • For each file or folder: a short description of what it contains
  • File format (if not obvious from the extension)
  • Relationships between files (e.g. which script processes which data file)
  • Date the file was created; date(s) of updates and what changed

Sharing and access information

  • Licence — the licence that applies to the data
  • Links to related publications that cite or use the data
  • Recommended citation for the dataset

Methodological information

  • Description of data collection or generation methods — link to protocols or publications where relevant
  • Data processing steps — how raw data was cleaned, transformed, or analysed
  • Software, instruments, and version numbers needed to open or run the files
  • Quality assurance procedures performed on the data

Data-specific information (repeat for each file or dataset as needed)

  • Variable list — full names and definitions of all column headings for tabular data
  • Units of measurement
  • Codes for missing data (e.g. NA, -999, null)
  • Specialised formats, abbreviations, or categorical codes used

docs.title: README Template — Get Inspired
docs.text:
The template below is written in Markdown (.md) — a lightweight plain text format that is both human-readable as raw text and renders nicely in most tools (GitHub, VS Code, data repositories, etc.). You do not need to know Markdown to use it: simply copy the template, open it in any text editor, and fill in your information.

A few formatting conventions used in the template:

  • ## Section headers — double # creates a section; use these to organise your README into logical parts
  • **bold text** — use for field labels or key terms
  • | tables | — use a Markdown table to list files, variables, or column descriptions; tables make this information much easier to scan than a plain list
  • `code` — wrap file names, variable names, and code in backticks so they stand out clearly

You can copy the full template or individual sections and adapt them to your dataset. Not all sections will apply to every project — remove what is not relevant and expand what matters most for your data.

Tip

Use the copy button (top right of the code block) to copy the full template to your clipboard in one click.

# README — [Dataset Title]

## General information

**Title:** [Dataset title]
**Authors:**
- Name, Affiliation, ORCID
- Name, Affiliation, ORCID

**Principal investigator / contact:** [Name, email]
**Date of data collection:** YYYY-MM-DD (or YYYY-MM-DD / YYYY-MM-DD)
**Geographic location:** [Location, if applicable]
**Funding:** [Funding agency and grant number, if applicable]

---

## Data and file overview

| File / Folder     | Description                    | Format      | Created    |
|---|---|---|---|
| `data/raw/`       | Raw instrument output          | .csv        | YYYY-MM-DD |
| `data/processed/` | Cleaned and processed data     | .csv        | YYYY-MM-DD |
| `scripts/`        | Analysis scripts               | .py / .R    | YYYY-MM-DD |
| `results/`        | Output figures and tables      | .png / .csv | YYYY-MM-DD |
| `README.md`       | This file                      | .md         | YYYY-MM-DD |

---

## Sharing and access information

**Licence:** [e.g. CC BY 4.0 — see LICENCE.txt for full terms]
**Related publication:** [Title, DOI]
**Recommended citation:** [Authors (Year). Title. Repository. DOI]

---

## Methodological information

**Data collection methods:**
[Brief description of how data was collected — instruments, protocols, experimental conditions]

**Data processing:**
[How raw data was cleaned, processed, or transformed]

**Software and dependencies:**
- [Software name, version]
- [Language: e.g. Python 3.11, R 4.3]

---

## Data-specific information

### [Filename or dataset name]

**Number of variables:** [N]
**Number of rows / observations:** [N]

| Variable | Full name   | Description | Units | Missing values |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `col1`   | Column one  | Description | unit  | NA             |
| `col2`   | Column two  | Description | unit  | NA             |

[Repeat for each file as needed]

A community-inspired template

This template was shaped by the interactions and support given to A-LIFE researchers over time. The questions asked, the datasets shared, and the feedback received from the A-LIFE community were invaluable in understanding what works in practice — and what researchers actually need when documenting their data. Thank you to everyone who contributed, knowingly or not, to making this resource better.

Tips for a good README

  • Write it before you upload — it forces you to think about what you are sharing and why
  • Copy the key description into the Zenodo or Yoda Description field so it is visible on the landing page
  • Include the README inside your ZIP archive and also upload it as a separate file
  • Use YYYY-MM-DD date formats throughout for consistency

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Well organised data is the foundation of good research data management — it makes your data easier to find, use, share, and preserve, both for yourself and others. This guide provides practical best practices for organising your research data files, specifically tailored for A-LIFE researchers.

The recommendations in this guide are particularly useful when working collaboratively, preparing data for transfer to Yoda, or getting ready to archive and publish. While this document focuses on digital data, the same principles can also apply to physical data objects such as microscope slides, sample jars, and other lab materials.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
During a research project, you will generate a large number of data files. How you organise these files should align with your research plan and reflects the workflow of your project. Grouping your files into organised folders will not only help keep your research work systematic, but also make it easier to locate files when needed. At the start of a project or study, you likely already have an idea of the types of data you will be working with, collecing and processing. This is a good time to begin structuring your folders to keep all your project files optimally well organised from the beginning.

While it may be tempting to simply dump all your files into one folder, a logical folder structure will make navigating your data easier and provide a clear overview of your files. This allows you to quickly find the right file or folder.

In this section, we provide practical tips on how to create a folder organisation scheme that best suits your project.

docs.title: Best Practices for a good project directory structure
docs.text:
1. Use simple and meaningful folder names
    • Use a systematic naming convention for consistency.
    • Use descriptive terms that help to reflect the folder's contents. For example the folder named "submitted" contains most likely final versions of manuscripts that have been submitted.
    • Apply the file naming best practices to folder names (see next section on File naming).

    Example of folder names that reflect what they contain1

  2. Group related files together
    • Organise files by data type (e.g., images, databases, DNA sequences).
    • Organise files by the kind of material they contain (e.g., publications, codes, literature or protocols).
    • Structure files based on research workflow activities. These could be a arranged by a specific event in a process or step in an experiment (e.g., input_images, process_step_initial and output_graphs)
    • Files that contain sensitive or personal data should be stored in separate folders with appropriate access controls and documentation.

    Example of where each folder stores files of the same type of data

  3. Structure folders hierarchically

    • Limit the number of high-level folders for broad topics, and more specific folders inside.
    • Avoid too many hierarchical layers, limit to 3-4 layers.
    • The main folder(s) should contain a name that reflects the project and relevant words that can be used to identify the dataset (e.g., Project, Person or Study name).
    • If managing multiple independent datasets, create separate subfolders for each.2.

    Example of a well-structured project directory

    project_name/
    code/               code needed to go from input files to final results
    data/               raw and primary data (never edit!)
        raw_external/
        raw_internal/
        metadata/
    doc/                documentation of the study  
    intermediate/       output files from intermediate analysis steps  
    logs/               logs from the different analysis steps  
    notebooks/          notebooks that document your day-to-day work  
    results/            output from workflows and analyses  
        figures/  
        reports/  
        tables/  
    scratch/            temporary files that can safely be deleted or lost  
    README.txt          file and folder description

  4. Folders should be distinct and non-redundant

    • group files into distinct categories without unnecessary overlap3.
    • each file should have only one logical location.
    • avoid duplicating folders with similar content, which can lead to confusion and version control issues.

    Example of a poor folder organisation due to redundancy4

  5. Document and share the file organisation scheme

    • Design and decribe your file organisation scheme including the folder structure, the folder contents and naming conventions.
    • Include the file organisation scheme in a README file (ideally in a text or markdown format) that is placed in the main folder of your project.
    • The documented scheme makes it easier for you and collaborators to navigate in the project directory and navigate the project.
    • README files and organisation scheme should be the first reference point when accessing the project directory.

    tip

    Read more and download this great README template5 to use for your folder.

Is there a difference between a folder and a directory?

The short answer is yes. While directory and folder are often be used interchangeably, they have distinct meanings:

  • Folder usually referes to the graphical user interface (GUI) term used in file explorers
  • Directory is more a file system term, often used in command-line environment.

Keep in mind that any folder can also be accessed as a directory. If one is referring to a container of documents, the term folder is more appropriate. The term directory refers to the way a structured list of document files and folders is stored on the computer. The distinction can be due to the way a directory is accessed; on Unix systems, /usr/bin/ is usually referred to as a directory path when viewed in a command line console, but if accessed through a graphical file manager, users may sometimes call it a folder.

Read more about the folder metaphor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A well structured file name is one of the most useful methods for keeping your data organised and you before anyone else will benefit from it. Think of file naming as the art of turning chaos into order. While naming files is often a personal choice, a logical and adaptable approach will help you quickly idenfity and remember a file's content.

This section outlines simple, effective rules to ensure a consistent and logical file naming scheme. Applying these best practices from the start, whether is for personal use only (e.g., your files on your laptop) or in share project environments (e.g., such a GitHub), can save you time and effort in the long run.

docs.title: What are the main advantages of using a consistent file naming strategy?
docs.text:
1. Enhance readability for yourself and others.
  2. Simplify your future tasks, suche as searching for a file or batch processing.
  3. Improving findability of files, thus reducing time spent searching for files and navigating through repositories.
  4. Identify contents quickly without opening every file to see what it contains.
  5. Facilitate collaboration by making files easy for others to understand.

docs.title: What makes a good file name?
docs.text:
A good file name satisfies these three key requirements: 1. It is human readable. 2. It is machine readable. 3. It supports logical ordering and sorting.

In the next sub-section, we outline practical rules to help you create an effective file naming convention or naming scheme.

docs.title: Best Practices for naming files
docs.text:
1. Keep it simple and consistent

    • Use clear, meaningful words in filenames that describe the content or purpose.
    • Use words or terms that are easy for you, and others, to understand.
    • Maintain a consistent naming pattern across similar files.

    Example of a consistent file list for experiments

    experiment01_temperature_readings_20250212.csv
experiment02_temperature_readings_20250212.csv
experiment01_temp_normalised_20250212.xlsx
experiment02_temp_normalised_20250212.xlsx

  2. Keep filenames short but descriptive

    • Use abbreviations (two or three letters) when needed. For example, use exp1 for experiment1.
    • Keep filenames under 32 characters for readability. For example, avoid this sort 'whyIsthisFilenameSolongIdidnotThink-This-Through.txt'
    • Main key details to include in filenames:
      • Date of creation (YYYYMMDD)
      • Project (name/number/experiment/acronym)
      • Type of data (Sample ID, Analysis, Conditions, Modifications, etc.)
      • Location
      • Creator (name/initials)
      • Version number
      • Reserve the last 3-letters for file format (such as .xls, .mov, .tif, .doc)

    Examples of including key elements for generating structured filenames

    • If your file contains information about: Honeybee project, experiment 2, done in Helsinki, data file created on 2 December 2020,

      • then a good filename is: '20201202_HB_EXP2_HEL_FLIGHT_V03.xls'
      • following the rule: Date_ProjectAbbreviation_ExperimentNumber_Location_TypeOfData_VersionNumber

    • Or you are dealing with: A cropped image of an ant head taken on the third of December 2020 by Meg Megson

      • A good filename is: '20201203_MM_HEAD_CROPPED_V1.psd'
      • The rule Key: Time_CreatorData_TypeModification_Version

  3. Use a naming convention that groups similar files.

    • Your naming convention can vary by file type. For example, one name convention could apply to your image files, another to raw data and another to processed data.
    • Note your conventions and store them within the folder for clarity.

  4. Use alpha-numerical characters

    • Stick to letters, numbers, hyphens (-) or underscores (_).
    • Avoid excessive brackets such as ({ [ ( < > ) ] }).
    • Avoid the use of special characters ( ~ ! @ # $ & % ^ * | ) as these may caouse errors in file paths.
    • Avoid the use of periods, commas and quotations ( . , " ') as these may confuse file extensions.
    • Avoid accented characters ( ù, à, ë, ç, .. ) as these can be interepreted differently on different operating systems and terminals.
    • Keep naming consistent and document exceptions when necessary.

    Examples of using hyphens for filenames and repository names

    • Filenames (for reports, documents, or human-readable files):

      species-diversity-analysis-20250127.csv
ocean-temperature-trends-report.pdf

    • Repository names

      ocean-biodiversity-mapping
genome-sequence-analysis-tool
wildbirds-tracking-pipeline

    Examples of using underscores for scripts, datasets and function names.

    • Datasets 

      plant_growth_experiment_results.csv
marine_ecosystem_data_2023.csv
marine_ecosystem_analysis_2024.csv
water_sample_collection.xls

    • Scripts and functions

      water_sample_process.py
biome_data_analysis.R
analyse_species_distribution()
calculate_growth_rate()

    Examples of filenames with problematic special characters.

    These may result from accidental typing, free-form naming, or even when your cat sat on the keyboard 

        checklist*/comeupwithabetterone!@VU.txt
    *important!!ˆ.docx
    DONOTshare!!@?.doc
    doc4=/'code".md
    Co0Kb0OKvoilà.html
    aaaaaaaaassddd....txt

    Tip

    hyphens are mostly used for human-readable files and repositories naming, while it is more common to see that scripts and datasets names often use underscores, avoiding command-line issues. You will notice that Life Science and bioinformatics fields have a tendency of using underscores (_) in their filenames.

  5. Avoid spaces

    • Avoid spaces in filenames as they can break tab completion and make working with files on a command line more difficult.
    • Instead use capital letters and/or underscores ( _ ) to separate words, terms or abbreviations used to construct a filename (For example: RenalCapsuleScan001, RenalCortexScan001, renal_cap_scan_001, renal_cor_scan_001.)
    • A common practice to use hyphens ( - ) to delimit words within a term and underscores to separate distinct terms. (For example: renal-capsule_scan_001.tiff).
    • Do not start or end filenames with spaces, periods, or hyphens as these can be accidentally introduced in graphical interfaces and may cause issues.

    Examples filenames with spaces

    These may seem human-friendly but are actually inconsistent, machine-unfriendly and also difficul to read. 

        Our project doc finalfinal.doc
    OurProjectDocument final laststage.doc
    projectfinalfinalfinalversion I promise.doc

    Untitled 123 copy.doc
    Untitled 123 copy 2.doc
    Untitled 123 copy 2-1.doc

  6. Use a logical ordering system for filenames

    • Think of one or more of the following that works best for you.
    • Alphabetical ordering: start filenames with main key search word for easier sorting based on term.

    Examples of alphabetical ordered filenames

    The files are ordered by the key term fieldwork:

        fieldwork_farm-adrianne
    fieldwork_farm-arianna
    fieldwork_farm-barbara
    fieldwork_farm-charlotte
    fieldwork_farm-clara
    • Numerical ordering: use leading zeros to maintain proper sorting. For example, for more than nine files, use left-zero padding to create a sorted sequence, for example, use 00, 05, 09, 10, 11, .. instead of the less intuitive 0, 10, 11, 5, 9, ...

    Examples of using numerical ordering

    Numbered filenames with left-zero padding (as 009 instead of 9). 

        figure008_scatterplot_COR10.png
    figure009_scatterplot_COR10.png
    figure010_scatterplot_COR10.png
    figure011_scatterplot_COR10.png
    • Chronological ordering: use the ISO 8601 standard dates format YYYYMMDD or YYYY-MM-DD and times, HH:MM:SS. For example: September 27, 2022 at 6 p.m. can be represented as 2022-09-27_18:00:00.000. Of course dates and times can also be used anywhere in the filename.

    Examples of using chronological ordering

    consistent date-based filenames following a chronological order. 

        2025-01-04_processed-data.csv
    2025-01-05_processed-data.csv
    2025-04-11_plasmidA01-mutant_H01.csv
    2025-04-11_plasmidA01-mutant_H02.csv
    2025-04-11_plasmidA01-mutant_H03.csv

    20260204_meeting-notes.doc
    20260206_meeting-notes.doc
    20260209_meeting-notes.doc

    Examples of inconsistent numbering

    If one is not consistent with the numbering rule, then this leads to incorrect sorting 

        copyfig 111.png
    fig 111.png
    figure 21.png
    fig22.png
    fig22copy2.png
    image11.png
    image1.png
    image9.png

    Tip

    • alphabetical and chronological ordering help track file versions.
    • numerical ordering ensures files are sorted logically.

  7. Filenames and file versions

    • Use versioning to indicate the current version and avoid confusion.
    • Add version numbers at the end of the filename, (for example: version 2 of the your file could be filename_v2.doc.
    • Use a consistent format such as using the leading v for v01 or v02, or ISO 8601 date and timestamps, such as YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS for precise tracking.

    Examples of versioning in filenames

    version label used in filenames, such as a format or date. 

        experiment_illumina_v01.csv
    experiment_illumina_v02.csv

    experiment_illumina_20260223.csv
    experiment_illumina_20260224.csv

  8. Document your naming conventions and patterns

    • Maintain a README file in your directory to define abbreviations and naming patterns.
    • Include explanations for abbreviations, formatting rules and your versioning methods.

    Examples of including a naming convention in documentation

    version label used in filenames, such as a format or date. 

    ## Abbreviations used in dataset A (.csv format), where header corresponds to column name

### column 1: title_name
P1 : Project_1
P2 : Project_2

### column 2: scientific_name 
MUS : Mus musculus
DRO : Drosophila

docs.title: Tips for maintaining good filenames
docs.text:
1. How is your file named?

    • Check how exported are automatically named by your tool. For example, Word applications may insert extra spaces or add the word copy).
    • Avoid accidental trailing spaces, check the names as they can be hard to spot on high-resolution monitors!

  2. Where did my file go?

    • Double check where a file is saved, some programs default to unexpected locations and you may lose track of the name.
    • Avoid typos and special characters that my cause errors in different operating systems. Some software, M$ Office comes to mind, tends to default where it thinks you should save a file. Don't let M$ dictate your workflow and navigate to where you want to save your file.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: File versioning helps manage multiple versions of files or drafts of your files. It is important for tracking changes, collaborations, and restoring previous versions if needed.

docs.title: What are the main advantages of versioning?
docs.text:
1. increases transparancy as you are able to track the changes and check what modifications were made, when and by whom.
  2. allows you to go back in case of errors, and modifications that were not wanted.
  3. improves also the collaborations and you can ensure that all the researchers point to the same (latest) version.

docs.title: Best Practices for a good file version
docs.text:
1. Use clear version numbers in filenames

    • Follow a structured versioning system. For example v1.0, v2.0, v1.1, and using the first number for major changes and the second for minor changes; v1_LP if you are working in a group and need to keep track of who made the changes.
    • use major.minor notation for small modifications, such as to distinguish between the copies 'rdm_documentation_v1.0' with 'rdm_documentation_v1.1' 6.
    • avoid unclear labelling such as finalfinal.doc or finalversion11.doc`.
    • optionally, add dates to show when a version was created or when a change has been made.

  2. Track who made changes

    • Add initials to filenames for shared files. For example rdm-documentation-v1.1_IM for Irene Martorelli editing the file.
    • Keep a document version log that documents what changed, when and by whom to keep track of the changes made beween version.

    Examples of a version log to keep track

    version table for tracing modification references used for a collaboration. 

        | Version | Date     | Author         | Changes                |
    |---------|----------|----------------|------------------------|
    | v0.1    | 20260202 | B. Olivier     | Initial draft          |
    | v0.2    | 20260212 | I. Martorelli  | Added examples         |
    | v0.3    | 20260213 | I. Martorelli  | Included a new section |

    Tip

    Check out this guide on versioning: Introduction to semantic versioning

docs.title: Best Practices — Completing the Yoda Metadata Form
docs.text:
A practical guide to completing the Yoda Metadata Form for A-LIFE researchers

Overview

This guide is part of Guides in the A-LIFE RDM GEMs collection.

This document provides best practices for completing each metadata field in the Yoda Metadata Form, required when submitting data for archiving. It is a companion to the workflow described in Archiving Data in Yoda.

Supporting materials: Archiving Data in Yoda Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-06-24 — Version: 1.2

Save frequently — sessions time out!

The Yoda portal session can time out while filling in the form. Click SAVE frequently (top left corner of the metadata form) to avoid losing your input.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The Yoda Metadata Form is attached to each folder in your Research Space. You can add metadata to the root folder of your project, or to each subfolder individually. The order of the fields in this guide follows the order of fields in the Yoda metadata form as accessed on 2025-07-18.

docs.title: Metadata Field occurrence mapping
docs.text:
Type Occurrence Definition Property Example Mandatory (1,1) Exactly one item is required Title Mandatory (1,N) At least one item is required, multiple values allowed Contributor Recommended (0,1) Optional, at most one item Version Recommended (0,N) Optional, multiple items allowed Discipline

All Mandatory fields are marked with an asterisk in the form.

docs.title: Title
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: A minimum description for the content in the datapackage

Type: Mandatory

Occurrence: 1,1

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Title
docs.text:
1. The Title should contain main keywords relevant to the data.
  2. Should not be longer than 255 characters.
  3. The Title is comprehensible to other disciplines, try to use more generic common words rather than specific, technical terms.
  4. Should not be a single, generic word. For example Dataset.
  5. Think of a catchy Title. A title is a good key to help others find you and your work.
  6. Make a Title distinguishable. Try not to use the same title for naming different datasets of the same collection.
  7. The Title does not begin with a backslash ( / ) and avoid using special characters, for examples, symbols such as #, $, /n.
  8. The Title should be written in the same language as the rest of the metadata fields.

docs.title: Examples of good and not so good Titles
docs.text: Good Title  This is concise, includes key terms that are related to the datapackage, keywords and description of the project and is understandable across disciplines. (ref: DOI) Good Title This contains explicit words. It is specific and part of social science and it is clear to other disciplines. (ref: DOI) Bad Title Title uses a set of acronyms that are difficult to comprehend what the datapackage is about. (ref: DOI) Bad Title This title is provided in dutch, while the rest of the metadata fields, including the abstract are provided in english. (ref: DOI)

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: A brief summary of the datapackage

Type: Mandatory

Occurrence: 1,1

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Description
docs.text:
1. The description is an abstract of the datapackage of a study, it should not describe a manuscript/article.
  2. A description is no longer than 2700 characters.
  3. The description should not contain the description of a README file (e.g. a full list of method parameters and values, and/or a pipeline description).
  4. Check typos as these are not controlled.

docs.title: Examples of good and not so good Descriptions
docs.text: Good Description  A clear summary to use for a Description. It does not contain specific details. The README file contains more details of the method and the parameters used (ref: DOI) Good Description  A clear description of the content within the datapackage. Results are not included here, but relevant resources are provided in the README file (ref: DOI). Good Description  Data content in relation to a publication is provided (ref: DOI) Bad description  the description is lengthy and detailed, with many parameters that distract the reader, making it hard to understand what the data is about (ref: DOI).

docs.title: Discipline
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The scientific branch associated to the datapackage

Type: Mandatory

Occurrence: 1,N

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Discipline
docs.text:
1. At least one sub-discipline should be provided for categorizing the research datapackage.
  2. It is recommended to look into the 6 main Disciplines classification used in Science (OECD, Revised field of Science and Technology (FOS) classification 2007) if there is uncertainty regarding which category the datapackage belongs to.
  3. More than one sub-discipline can be added by selecting the ( + ) button.
  4. In general, data of A-LIFE falls into: "1. Natural Sciences" and "3. Medical and Health Sciences".

docs.title: Version
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: Assigning a number that identifies the status of the development of the resource

Type: Recommended

Occurrence: 0,1

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Version number
docs.text:
1. It is highly recommended to provide the Version value = 1.0.0 when submitting the datapackage for the first time.
  2. For each sequential minor change, increment the Version number (e.g. 1.1.0 follows 1.0.0).
  3. A Version should be provided when there are minor content changes.

Tip

Read more about versioning: Introduction to semantic versioning

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: Is the main language of the data package

Type: Mandatory

Occurrence: 1,1

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Language selection
docs.text:
1. One Language needs to be selected from the drop down menu; by default English is selected.
  2. The reference list follows ISO 639-1 standard names.
  3. The same language should be used across all metadata fields, in particular Title, Description, and the README file.

docs.title: Collection Process
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: A date range that provides the duration of the data collection for the datapackage

Type: Recommended

Occurrence: 0,1

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Collection Process range
docs.text:
1. Use the calendar to select the Start date — a close estimate of when work on the data started.
  2. Select an End date when data collection is complete.
  3. Make sure the date range follows chronological order — the End date cannot be earlier than the Start date.

docs.title: Location(s) covered
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: A geographical place that is associated to the data package.

Type: Recommended

Occurrence: 0,N

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Location
docs.text:
1. Free text field — make sure the spelling is correct.
  2. Provide the name(s) of the location(s) where data was collected, generated, or where experiments were conducted.
  3. More than one Location can be provided using the (+) symbol.
  4. It is recommended to provide location names in English.

Tip

Use Getty Thesaurus of Geographic Names to look up reference geographic names.

docs.title: Period covered
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: A date range that provides the duration period of working on the data

Type: Recommended

Occurrence: 0,1

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Period Covered
docs.text:
1. Start date — when work on the data started (e.g. project start date).
  2. End date — can be the actual date of submission of the data package in Yoda.
  3. Make sure the dates follow chronological order.

docs.title: Keywords
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: Keywords associated to the datapackage that increase discoverability.

Type: Recommended

Occurrence: 0,N

Warning

Please note that the field name Tags has been renamed to Keywords.

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Keyword
docs.text:
1. Use Keyword terms that help to find your work.
  2. A Keyword can consist of one or multiple words.
  3. Avoid using commas , or semicolons ; to separate keywords — they will not be parsed as distinct terms.
  4. Use the plus button ( + ) to add each keyword separately.
  5. Include keywords associated to the Title and Description.
  6. Keywords longer than 255 characters will raise an error.
  7. Do not use parameter-style values (e.g. mean, 2.5, 2x).
  8. Avoid acronyms and abbreviations that are not unique across disciplines.
  9. Check typos and avoid special characters (#, $, /n, !, "", &).

docs.title: Examples of good and not so good Keywords
docs.text: Good Keywords  Distinct tags relevant to the datapackage and terms from the title. (DOI) Good Keywords  Keywords added with the " + " option, relevant to the datapackage. (DOI) Keywords not parsed  Keywords separated with " ; " — not parsed as distinct terms. (DOI) Keywords not useful for searching  Keywords are function/condition values — too specific to be useful for search. (DOI)

docs.title: Related resources
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: Used for referencing the current data package to other (related) works

Type: Recommended

Occurrence: 0,N

Warning

Please note that Related datapackages (Identifiers) has been renamed to Related resource.

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Related resource
docs.text:
1. Provide an associated related resource — a publication, website, or other digital source relevant to the data.
  2. When providing a Related resource, the fields Relation type, Title and Persistent Identifier are mandatory.
  3. Relation type is selected from the drop down menu (DataCite Relation Types).
  4. Title is the name of the resource (max 255 characters).
  5. Persistent Identifier requires a Type and an Identifier (URL). Use HTTPS.
  6. Multiple resources can be added using the ( + ) button.

Tip

Recommended Relation Type values: IsSupplementTo, IsSupplementBy, IsPartOf, HasPart (Source: DataCite relationType)

docs.title: Example of a good Related resource
docs.text:
How to provide a good Related resource

Provide the full URL for the Identifier so it can be resolved. In this example the related resource is a published manuscript.

How it looks once published

The DOI is resolved and visible in the published metadata. (DOI)

docs.title: Retention period
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The minimal number of years the data will be kept in archive.

Type: Mandatory

Occurrence: 1,1

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Retention period
docs.text:
1. Insert an integer value for Retention period.
  2. The default is 10 years. This is recommended for unpublished data; a shorter period can be specified, at minimum for the duration of the project.
  3. Data that is published must be archived for a minimum of 10 years.

docs.title: Retention information
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: Extra information regarding the retention period

Type: Mandatory

Occurrence: 1,1

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Retention information
docs.text:
1. Free text field — keep it clear and without typos.
  2. If the Retention period is modified from the default (10 years), provide a justification here.
  3. Should not be longer than 255 characters.

docs.title: Embargo end date
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: A period during which a published dataset remains unavailable to the public.

Type: Recommended

Occurrence: 0,1

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Embargo end date
docs.text:
1. Only required when an embargo applies — leave blank otherwise.
  2. The default date is the current date.
  3. The date must be chronologically after the submission date.

Warning

The Embargo end date will not appear in the published metadata — it is used by administrators only to know when data can be released.

docs.title: Data type
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The type of the data contained in the datapackage.

Type: Mandatory

Occurrence: 1,1

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Data Type
docs.text:
1. Selected from the scroll down menu.
  2. Options: Datapackage, Method, Software, or Other Document.
  3. Datapackage is the default and recommended unless the folder contains only a method or software.

docs.title: Data classification
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: A category level of sensitivity given to the data in case of data loss or theft.

Type: Mandatory

Occurrence: 1,1

Warning

VU Yoda no longer uses Low, Medium, High and Very High. Classification now aligns with Utrecht University.

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Data classification
docs.text:
1. Selected from the scroll down menu: Public, Basic, Sensitive or Critical.
  2. For most A-LIFE research data, the classification is Public.
  3. When Public, the Data Package Access should be set to Open - freely retrievable.
  4. When Sensitive/Critical, contact the RDM team to discuss a custom storage solution.

Data classification examples

VU classification Example Public publicly shared information, e.g. on a website Basic internal use, shared within your group/institution Sensitive health information, patient data Critical passwords, royal/military data, federal tax data

docs.title: Name of collection
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The name of the main collection the data package belongs to.

Type: Recommended

Occurrence: 0,1

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Name of collection
docs.text:
1. Ensure all data packages in the same Collection use the same Name of collection. This can be the Project Name.
  2. Free text field, max 255 characters.

docs.title: Funding reference
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The name(s) of the funding organisation(s)

Type: Recommended

Occurrence: 0,N

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Funding reference
docs.text:
1. Requires two fields: Funder and Award number (max 255 characters each).
  2. The same Funder can have multiple Award number(s) — add each with the ( + ) symbol.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: Important information about the datapackage for administrators

Type: Recommended

Occurrence: 0,1

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Remark
docs.text:
1. Max 2700 characters.
  2. When data access is Restricted, it is required to provide a contact person's full name and email address here.
  3. This information will not be published — it is used by administrators only.
  4. The datapackage manager and PI should be listed as contact persons.

docs.title: Example of a good Remark
docs.text:
A good remark

Full name and email address of a permanent project leader is provided.

docs.title: Creator
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The author of the research data — the main person who worked on the data.

Type: Mandatory

Occurrence: 1,N

Warning

With the updated Yoda metadata form, it is now possible to automatically retrieve the ROR identifier when an Affiliation name is selected.

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Creator
docs.text:
1. Required attributes: Name, Affiliation and Person Identifier.
  2. Given Name = first name (and middle names); Family Name includes prefixes (e.g. "van Rijn").
  3. Select the Affiliation name from the dropdown — the ROR identifier is then auto-filled.
  4. For VU-affiliated creators, select Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam.
  5. It is highly recommended to provide an ORCID for each creator.
  6. The order of creators follows the order of authorship, as in a manuscript.

Available Person identifier Types in Yoda

Person identifier Type Comment ORCID Open Researcher and Contributor ID DAI Digital Author Identifier — unique national number for Dutch university researchers Scopus Abstract and citation database identifier ResearcherID (Web of Science) Unique identifier across the Web of Science ecosystem ISNI ISO certified global standard number for contributors to creative works

Source: Datacite nameIdentifierScheme

docs.title: Contributor
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: A person analogous to a co-creator, listed in the Acknowledgements of a manuscript.

Type: Optional

Occurrence: 0,N

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Contributor
docs.text:
1. A Contributor is someone who would appear in the Acknowledgements of a manuscript, not listed as Creator.
  2. If a person is both a Creator and a Contributor, list them only as Creator.
  3. The same name and affiliation rules as for Creator apply.
  4. It is good practice to include the Project Leader and/or Supervisor(s) as contributors.
  5. The Contributor type specifies the role — select from the dropdown.

Tip

See Datacite — List Values Contributor Types for definitions of all contributor roles.

docs.title: Data Package Access
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: How the data will be accessible once archived.

Type: Mandatory

Occurrence: 1,1

Warning

Data Package Restriction has been renamed to Data Package Access as of 2025-07-01.

docs.title: Best Practices for a good Data Package Access
docs.text:
1. Options: Open - freely retrievable, Restricted - available upon request, Closed.
  2. Select Open when data is classified as Public — data will be publicly accessible.
  3. Where possible, non-sensitive data should be made Open.
  4. When Restricted, provide a contact person in the Remarks field and in the Custom License.
  5. When Closed, only the metadata will be visible — the data itself will not be accessible.

docs.title: License
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The license under which the data package is made available to third parties.

Type: Mandatory

Occurrence: 1,1

docs.title: Best Practices for selecting a license
docs.text:
1. Selected from the scroll down menu.
  2. Recommended: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International Public License — CC BY 4.0.
  3. When a license is selected from the menu, the license file is automatically included in the data package.
  4. When Custom is selected, you must manually add a license.txt file to the data package.

Check data accessibility and license

If Restricted or Closed is selected in Data package access, the only available license option is Custom.

Refer to the VU RDM Manual — License templates for the VU Restricted license template and VU Closed license template.

Not sure which license to pick?

For an overview of common research data licenses and what they mean, see the Licenses page in GEMs Essentials.

docs.title: Best Practices — Requesting Yoda Space
docs.text:
Overview

This guide is part of the Guides in the A-LIFE RDM GEMs collection.

This document provides best practices for completing the metadata fields in the Request Yoda Space form. It is a companion to the workflow described in Getting Started with Yoda.

Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-06-22 — Version: 0.4.1

Tip

The metadata fields listed here are based on the Request Storage Form accessed on 2026-01-30. Please ensure all mandatory fields are completed. Double-check free-text fields for typos before submitting.

docs.title: Register ticket on behalf of
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The person for whom the Yoda storage space is being requested. Type: Mandatory

  1. Provide the complete Given Name and Family Name of the person requesting space.
  2. If affiliated with VU, suggestions will appear as you type — select your name from the list.

docs.title: Project Owner
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The person responsible for the project and its data. Type: Mandatory

  1. Provide the complete Given Name and Family Name of the Project Owner.
  2. This is usually the Principal Investigator (PI) or head of the group responsible for the project and its funding.
  3. The Project Owner is the administrator of the storage space and can add and assign permissions to other users.
  4. If affiliated with VU, suggestions will appear as you type.

docs.title: Project Owner ORCID
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The ORCID persistent identifier of the Project Owner. Type: Recommended

  1. Insert the complete 16-digit identifier with hyphens every 4 digits: 0000-0000-0000-0001.
  2. The field does not accept ORCIDs in URL form (e.g. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3929-0423 will raise an error).
  3. The field accepts X as a last digit (e.g. 0000-0003-3674-598X).
  4. Avoid using the letter O instead of the digit 0.
  5. Do not add trailing spaces — these will raise an error.

Warning

Make sure there are no spaces after the ORCID.

docs.title: Will the project owner also manage the data in Yoda?
docs.text:
1. Yes — the Project Owner and Project Manager are the same person.
  2. No — a separate Project Manager field will appear and must be completed.

docs.title: Project Manager
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The person directly involved in managing the data in the Yoda storage space. Type: Mandatory (only if delegated)

  1. Provide the complete Given Name and Family Name.
  2. The Project Manager will be made Group Manager in Yoda with the same admin permissions as the Project Owner.

docs.title: Project Manager ORCID
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The ORCID persistent identifier of the Project Manager. Type: Recommended

Same rules as Project Owner ORCID.

Further reading

Curious about how ORCID identifiers are structured? See Structure of ORCID Identifiers by Geoffrey Bilder.1

docs.title: What is the name of the project?
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: Title and description of the project. Type: Mandatory

  1. Provide the complete title of the project and relevant information.
  2. Treat it as a short abstract — include relevant keywords, affiliation if applicable.

docs.title: Project Abbreviation
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The short name used as the root folder name in Yoda. Type: Mandatory

  1. Should not exceed 40 characters.
  2. Use hyphens (-) to separate keywords.
  3. Use lowercase letters and numbers only — avoid special characters (~ ! @ # $ & % ^ * |).
  4. Use a recognisable name, e.g. salt-lakes-project or alien-variant-proteins.

Important

For A-LIFE researchers, your Yoda project folder will have the prefix research-beta-alife- added automatically. For example, salt-lakes-project becomes research-beta-alife-salt-lakes-project.

docs.title: Faculty
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The faculty division at VU to which this project belongs. Type: Mandatory

  1. Select one faculty from the list (names are in Dutch).
  2. For A-LIFE, select Faculteit der Bètawetenschappen — type BET to find it quickly.

docs.title: Department
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The department within the faculty. Type: Mandatory

  1. For A-LIFE, select Amsterdam Institute for Life and Environment.
  2. Start typing Ams (not A-LI or ALI) to find it in the list.

docs.title: Affiliate department or research institute
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The research institute name. Type: Mandatory

  1. For A-LIFE, select Amsterdam Institute for Life and Environment | beta-alife.
  2. Type ali or ALI to find it (unlike the Department field, this works here).

docs.title: Budget number type
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The fund type responsible for reporting the project. Type: Mandatory

  1. Select Cost center or WBS-Element.
  2. Your Budget holder can tell you which type and number applies to your project.

docs.title: Budget holder
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The person managing the project budget. Type: Recommended

  1. Contact your Budget holder if you are unsure of the budget number type or fund number.

docs.title: Project end date
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: The estimated date by which the project will be completed. Type: Recommended

  1. Use the format DD-MM-YYYY.
  2. This can usually be found in your grant documentation.
  3. This field is not controlled, so make sure that the date inserted is not in the past.

docs.title: Are you storing sensitive data?
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: Whether the data contains personal or sensitive information. Type: Recommended

  1. Default is No. Select Yes if the data is sensitive.
  2. When Yes is selected, specify the type: identifiable personal data, copyrighted data, confidential data, or anonymised personal data.

Not sure how to classify your data?

Use the VU Basic Research Data Classification Tool.

docs.title: Have you contacted a Data Steward / Privacy Champion?
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: Whether a data expert has been consulted. Type: Mandatory

  1. Select Yes if you have already contacted a Data Steward or Privacy Champion.
  2. If not, contact the A-LIFE RDM team before submitting.

docs.title: Storage volume required
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: Estimated volume of data to be stored. Type: Mandatory

  1. Provide a realistic estimate of the total data volume for the project.
  2. For more information on storage costs, see the VU Storage Cost Model.

What are the costs for active storage in Yoda?

Volume Active storage cost 0 – 500 GB Free (covered by VU) 501 GB – 1 TB €200 per TB per year 1 TB – 2 TB €250 per TB per year > 2 TB Not covered — contact RDM support

docs.title: Do you expect to archive (part of) the data in Yoda?
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: Indication of intended use of the Yoda space. Type: Recommended

  1. Select Yes if you expect to archive data in Yoda.
  2. Select No if you plan to use Yoda as active storage only.
  3. Select Maybe if you are not yet sure.

docs.title: Do you expect to publish (part of) the data in Yoda?
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: Indication of whether data will be published. Type: Recommended

  1. Select Yes if you plan to publish data in Yoda.
  2. Select No if data will not be published.

docs.title: Yoda usage agreement
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: Agreement to iRODS/Yoda Terms of Use. Type: Mandatory

  1. Check the I agree box before submitting.
  2. Read the Yoda Terms of Use (version 1.0.0) before agreeing.

docs.title: Yoda Intake — Would you like someone to contact you?
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: Request for onboarding support. Type: Optional

  1. Select No if you do not need help getting started.
  2. Select Yes to schedule an intake session.

Recommendation for A-LIFE researchers

We recommend selecting No here and contacting the A-LIFE RDM team directly — they can provide more targeted support than the faculty-level intake.

docs.title: Additional information
docs.text:
Metadata

Definition: Free-text field for any extra remarks. Type: Optional

  1. Use this field for any comments or project-specific information the RDM support team should be aware of.
  2. You may also attach relevant documents to the form.

  1. Structure of the ORCID Identifier, Geoffrey Bilder — view document ↩

docs.title: BP — Zenodo — Metadata Form
docs.text:
Overview

This is the BP — Zenodo — Metadata Form guide, part of GEMs → Guides in the A-LIFE RDM collection.

This document provides best practices for completing the metadata fields in Zenodo. Fields are grouped into three categories:

  • Basic Information — Mandatory
  • Recommended Information — Highly recommended
  • Other Information — Optional but good practice

Supporting materials: GEMs — Licences, GEMs — PIDs Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-02-20 — Version: 0.6.0

docs.title: 1. Basic Information
docs.text:
Basic Information

Definition: Minimum description of the data package — visible once published. Type: Mandatory — complete all fields.

docs.title: Digital Object Identifier — Mandatory
docs.text:
• Reserve a DOI before publishing by clicking Get a DOI now! — the DOI is registered only when the record is published.
  • If you select Yes, do not provide a DOI linked to a journal article. Instead, add the article DOI in the Related works field.

docs.title: Resource Type — Mandatory
docs.text:
• Select Dataset for data files (e.g. CSV, XLS) and for data that includes scripts.
  • Select Software when publishing a software package or a specific version of a code repository.

docs.title: Title — Mandatory
docs.text:
• Provide a title that reflects the content of the data. The title is used in citations and for discovery.
  • Keep it concise. Use Add additional title/subtitle for very long titles.
  • A good format for datasets: "Dataset for [Title of your article]"
  • Avoid special characters (e.g. # % & @).

docs.title: Publication Date — Mandatory
docs.text:
• Defaults to the date the draft was created. Can be modified.
  • Use ISO format: YYYY-MM-DD.

docs.title: Creator — Mandatory
docs.text:
• A Creator is an author of the dataset and is included in the citation.
  • Search by ORCID to auto-populate name and affiliation.
  • It is highly recommended to provide an ORCID and a ROR affiliation for each Creator. The affiliation field is auto-completed from the ROR database.

docs.title: Description — Mandatory
docs.text:
• Provide a paragraph or short summary describing your dataset — it appears under the title once published.
  • Do not copy the abstract of your article — the Description should specifically describe the dataset.
  • The Description is not a substitute for a README file: the Description gives a general summary; the README describes the content of individual files.

A good example

See a good Description example from an A-LIFE researcher: Zenodo dataset.

docs.title: Licence — Mandatory
docs.text:
• A licence is required for others to reuse your data. By default, CC BY 4.0 is applied.
  • For datasets, see How do I licence my research data?.
  • For software, see Choose a Licence.
  • For an overview of common licences, see our GEMs — Licences page.

docs.title: Copyright — Recommended
docs.text: • A copyright statement describing ownership of the uploaded resource. By default: Copyright © (2025) The Authors.

docs.title: 2. Recommended Information
docs.text:
Recommended Information

Definition: Not strictly required to publish, but highly recommended for a complete and well-documented record. Type: Recommended

docs.title: Contributors — Optional
docs.text:
• Add Contributors in the same way as Creators — they are not included in the citation.
  • Do not add a person as a Contributor if they are already listed as a Creator.
  • Assign a Role (e.g. Supervisor, Contact person, Sponsor) — equivalent to someone you would include in manuscript Acknowledgements.

docs.title: Keywords and Subjects — Optional but highly recommended
docs.text:
• Keywords are free-form text; Subjects are from controlled vocabularies (e.g. Medical Subject Headings — MeSH).
  • Press Enter or click Add after each term to create separate tags — do not enter all terms as one string.
  • Check if your term is already in the European Science Vocabulary (EuroSciVoc) — shown as EuroSciVoc in the dropdown.
Selecting keywords and subjects from standard vocabularies

docs.title: Languages — Optional
docs.text: • More than one language can be selected.

docs.title: Dates — Optional
docs.text:
• Add specific date types beyond the publication date (e.g. submission or acceptance dates for preprints).
  • Use ISO format: YYYY-MM-DD.

docs.title: Version — Recommended
docs.text:
• For a first publication, use 1.0.0.
  • Increment the version number for each subsequent update (e.g. 1.1.0 follows 1.0.0).

Semantic versioning

See Introduction to semantic versioning for guidance on versioning datasets and software.

docs.title: Publisher — Optional
docs.text: • The Publisher appears in the citation. Zenodo is the default and will be visible in your record's citation. You may replace it with your institution's name.

docs.title: 3. Other Information
docs.text:
Other Information

Definition: Additional contextual information. Not mandatory, but recommended if the information exists. Type: Optional

docs.title: Funding — Optional but recommended
docs.text:
• Provide funding information for awards and grants associated with your research.
  • Standard award/grant: click + Add.
  • Custom award/grant: click + Add Custom — the funder must be registered in ROR.
  • More than one funding source can be added.

docs.title: Related works — Optional but highly recommended
docs.text:
• Use this field to cross-link your dataset with related publications, datasets, or other resources.
  • Mandatory sub-fields: Relation type, Identifier, and Scheme.
  • The most common relation type for datasets is Is Supplement To (links your dataset to a related article).
  • See the full list of DataCite Relation Types.

docs.title: References — Optional
docs.text: • Prefer using Related works to cross-link resources rather than this field.

docs.title: Software — Optional
docs.text:
• Relevant for Software resource types. Sub-fields: Repository URL, Programming language, and Repository status (e.g. Active).

Using GitHub with Zenodo?

Zenodo integrates with GitHub to automatically archive repository versions. See Referencing content on GitHub and Zenodo GitHub and Software.

docs.title: Publishing information — Optional
docs.text: • Relevant for manuscripts uploaded to Zenodo. Fields include Journal, Book, etc.

docs.title: Conference — Optional
docs.text: • Relevant for conference-related outputs (posters, presentations). Include the conference name and location.

docs.title: Domain specific fields — Optional
docs.text:
• Include domain-specific metadata where applicable.

What next?

Metadata complete! Head back to Archiving in Zenodo and continue to the publishing step.

  1. GitHub Docs — Referencing and citing content: https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/archiving-a-github-repository/referencing-and-citing-content ↩

  2. Zenodo Documentation — GitHub and Software: https://help.zenodo.org/docs/github/ ↩
