docs.title: Data Transfer Options, Tips and Solutions
docs.text:
meta

This document is part of the A-LIFE GEMs (Guides, Essentials & Manuals) Collection. This section is part of Manuals -> Yoda -> Transfering data with Cyberduck.

Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier, version 0.2.3, 2025-11-11

docs.title: Cyberduck
docs.text:
When you want to transfer data that has a volume more than 20MB, or more than one data file at once, it is highly recommended to use Cyberduck for accessing Yoda and transfering data from your device. In this document we provide 10 steps to start with Cyberduck.

Please be aware that you need to have access to Yoda via the portal in order to transfer data. If you do not have access to the Yoda portal, please make sure to request storage space [add guide link] or ask permission to the Yoda data project owner to grant you access to the space

docs.title: ✅ 10 Simple Steps for connecting to Yoda with Cyberduck
1. Download Cyberduck Tool
docs.text:
• For Windows users, go to https://cyberduck.io/download/ and download Cyberduck.
  • For MacOS users, there are two options: download it directly from https://cyberduck.io/download/ or search Cyberduck in the VU Software Center Tool and install it in your device. If you do not have VU Software Center Tool you can download it from: https://munki.mac.vu.nl/installers/.

docs.title: 2. Sign in to the Yoda Portal
docs.text:
• Go to: https://portal.yoda.vu.nl
  • Sign in by using your-username@vu.nl and VU password.

docs.title: 3. Generate a new Data Access Password
docs.text:
• Go to: https://portal.yoda.vu.nl/user/data_access
  • Click Generate new data access password
  • For the Label option, type: Cyberduck
  • Click Generate data access password

docs.title: 4. Copy the password
docs.text: • Highlight the generated password and press Command + C to copy.

docs.title: 5. Open Cyberduck and add a new bookmark
docs.text:
• Click the Bookmarks icon of Cyberduck
  • Then click the + button

docs.title: 6. Choose WebDAV (HTTPS) as connection type
docs.text: • Select WebDAV (HTTPS) protocol from the dropdown option list.

docs.title: 7. Fill in the connection details:
docs.text:
• Server: data.yoda.vu.nl
  • Username: your-username@vu.nl
  • Password: paste (Command + v) the password you generated in point 3.

docs.title: 8. Close the bookmark window
docs.text: • Click the X to return to the main Cyberduck home window.

docs.title: 9. Connect to Yoda
docs.text:
• Your new bookmark (data.yoda.vu.nl - WebDAV (HTTPS)) is visible in the home window.
  • Click to the Yoda bookmark to connect and access your Yoda folders.
  • You may need to add your VU password when trying to connect for the first time. Save it for next time.

docs.title: 10. Manage your project directory via the Cyberduck interface
docs.text:
• you can drap and drop files and foleds from your laptop directories to your Yoda project repository.
  • a transfer window keeps open until the full transfer is complete
  • the same operation (from Yoda project directory) to your laptop folders for dragging folders can be repeaded

Warning

Please note that the Data Access Password is valid for 90 days. After that, it expires and you will not be able to login in with Cyberduck. To regain access, simply repeat Steps [3 - 6] for generating a new password and update it in your Cyberduck bookmark.

Info

For more information please take a look at the VU RDM manual - Yoda using Cyberduck

docs.title: Manual — Create an eduID
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Create an eduID manual, part of GEMs → Manuals in the A-LIFE RDM collection.

This manual explains how to create an eduID account, which is required to access Yoda if your institution is not listed in the SRAM institutions list.

Related documentation: Manage Group Members in Yoda

Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-06-29 — Version: 0.1.0

docs.title: What is eduID?
docs.text:
eduID is a digital identity provided by SURF that gives you a way to log in to websites and other online services in the Netherlands. With your eduID you can access administrative and educational processes at Dutch research and education institutions — even if you are not directly affiliated with one. It is designed for users whose institution is not part of the SRAM network, or who have no current institutional affiliation.

We recommend using the eduID app, as it is the most secure and convenient option. The app lets you log in without a password, and two-factor authentication (2FA) provides an extra layer of security.

More information: eduid.nl

docs.title: When should you create an eduID?
docs.text:
You need an eduID when you have been invited to a Yoda Research Space but are unable to log in because your institution is not listed among the organisations supported by SRAM.

This is typically the case when:

  • Your institution is not a Dutch research or education organisation
  • Your institution is a Dutch organisation but is not yet connected to SRAM
  • You are an independent researcher or freelancer with no current institutional affiliation

Before creating an eduID, check whether your institution is already supported by SRAM by consulting the list of institutions using SRAM (last accessed: 2026-06-29). If your institution appears in the list, you do not need an eduID — you can log in directly using your institutional credentials.

If your institution is not in the list, or if you try to log in and are redirected to an unfamiliar page without a recognisable login option, then creating an eduID is the recommended solution.

docs.title: Steps to create an eduID
docs.text:
1. Go to the eduID registration page — visit eduid.nl and click Create an eduID.

    Figure 1: Creating an eduID account

  2. Register your account — provide your email address and follow the steps to set up your account, including Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA).

    Use an account you can always access

    Make sure you register your eduID with an email address you can always access. Avoid using an institutional email address from another affiliation, as you may lose access to it in the future (e.g. when leaving an institution). Use a personal email address instead.

Further reading

SRAM invitations and eduID activation — VU Research Support Handbook eduID — SURF IAM documentation eduID support (English)

docs.title: Connect to Research Drive with Cyberduck
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Connect to Research Drive with Cyberduck manual, part of Manuals in the A-LIFE RDM GEMs collection.

This document covers how to connect to your Research Drive project space using Cyberduck via WebDAV and transfer data.

Supporting materials: Research Drive — Transferring Data Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-06-25 — Version: 0.1.0

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Cyberduck is a free desktop client (Windows and macOS) that connects to Research Drive via WebDAV, allowing you to upload, download, and manage your files with a simple drag-and-drop interface.

Before you start

You need to have access to a Research Drive project space before you can connect. If you do not have access yet, see Getting Started with Research Drive.

docs.title: Steps for Connecting to Research Drive with Cyberduck
1. Download Cyberduck
docs.text: • Download Cyberduck from https://cyberduck.io/download/ (Windows and macOS).

docs.title: 2. Sign in to Research Drive
docs.text:
• Go to: https://vu.data.surfsara.nl
  • Sign in using your VU credentials.

docs.title: 3. Generate a WebDAV access token
docs.text:
• In Research Drive, open your Personal Settings and navigate to Security (or use this direct link: Security Settings).
Security setting option in the Research Drive main menu.
  • Scroll to App passwords / tokens.
  • Enter a name for your token (e.g. Cyberduck) and click Create new app passcode.
Security key section for generating a new passcode.

docs.title: 4. Save your credentials

docs.title: What is a Research Tool?
docs.text:
According to SURF, a research tool is a service that supports one or more stages of the research lifecycle — from data collection and processing to analysis, collaboration, publication, and preservation.1

Storage is one of the most fundamental components of research data management: it determines where your data lives while you are working on it, how it is shared with collaborators, and ultimately where it will be safely preserved at the end of your project. Not all storage is the same: active storage is where your data is created and used day-to-day, while archive storage is where your finalised data is deposited for the long term and made findable and reusable through a persistent identifier such as a DOI.

Alongside storage, there are tools that help you move data around — between your computer and a storage platform, between collaborators, or from one system to another. These transfer tools are not storage solutions themselves, but they are an essential part of getting your data where it needs to be, safely and efficiently.

In this documentation we currently focus on the tools supported at the VU, and we hope to expand coverage in the future. We also include other tools that are widely used in the A-LIFE environment and are accepted, secure, and well-established in the research community.

docs.title: Tool Classification in this RDM Collection
docs.text:
The table below gives an overview of the tools covered in this documentation, their category, and whether they are officially supported at the VU. VU Supported ✅ means the tool is listed on the VU Storage Finder.

  • Active Storage — the digital space where you keep your research data while actively working on it. The right solution depends on data volume, sensitivity, access frequency, and collaboration needs.
  • Archive Storage (Archiving & Publishing) — platforms for depositing finalised datasets for long-term preservation and making them publicly available with a persistent identifier such as a DOI. Unlike active storage, these are not designed for working files.
  • Transfer — tools for moving data between your local machine and a storage or archiving platform, or for sending large files securely to collaborators. They are not storage solutions themselves — they are the means by which you get data in and out of them.

docs.title: What is SURFfilesender?
docs.text:
SURFfilesender is a secure file transfer service provided by SURF that allows you to share large files easily and securely. The recipient does not need an account to download files — they simply receive a link and can access the data directly. This makes it ideal for sharing data with external collaborators, reviewers, or anyone outside your institution.

Available to all VU affiliated staff and students

Log in with your VU institution account via SURFconext: filesender.surf.nl

docs.title: How to use SURFfilesender
docs.text:
For step-by-step instructions on how to transfer data with SURFfilesender, see the dedicated manual:

Transfer data with SURFfilesender

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
• Share files up to 1 TB in size
  • Works via your web browser — no software or plugins needed
  • Recipient does not need an account
  • Two sharing options: by email or via an anonymous link
  • End-to-end encryption available for extra security
  • Links are valid for a defined period of time, with a maximum of 30 days
  • Files are stored in the Netherlands

docs.title: When to use SURFfilesender?
docs.text:
SURFfilesender is a good option in situations such as:

  • Your data needs to be reviewed for a journal — the journal requests access to your dataset during peer review, but your data is not yet publicly available
  • Your DOI is not yet created or not yet resolving — your dataset may not yet be archived or published, or the DOI exists but is temporarily not resolving due to a technical issue; SURFfilesender provides a secure temporary alternative while waiting for the issue to be fixed
  • You need to share data anonymously — the recipient should not know who is sharing the data, for example during double-blind review
  • The recipient has no account on Research Drive or Yoda — and creating one is not practical for a one-off transfer
  • You need to transfer a large file quickly — without setting up a shared folder or storage space

docs.title: Data sensitivity
docs.text:
SURFfilesender is primarily used for sharing sensitive data that cannot be shared via open platforms. However, always verify that sharing the data via this service complies with your data management plan and any applicable agreements.

Check your data sharing conditions

Before sharing sensitive or personal data, make sure you are authorised to share it and that the recipient is entitled to receive it. If in doubt, contact the A-LIFE Data Steward.

docs.title: What is Zenodo?
docs.text:
Zenodo is a free and open digital archive built by CERN and OpenAIRE, enabling researchers to share and preserve research outputs of any size, format, and from all fields of research.2 Launched in May 2013, it was originally developed to support the European Commission's Open Data policy as a catch-all repository for EC-funded research.

Zenodo accepts a wide range of research outputs:

  • Datasets — tabular data, observational data, experimental results
  • Software — code, scripts, analysis pipelines, specific repository versions
  • Publications — preprints, reports, theses
  • Presentations and posters — conference materials
  • Other — images, videos, interactive notebooks, and more

Zenodo imposes no requirements on format, size, access restrictions, or licence — removing barriers to sharing for researchers in any discipline. Every record receives a DOI, and metadata is automatically registered with DataCite and integrated into OpenAIRE reporting lines to funding agencies.

According to the VU Research Data and Software Management Policy, all research data and software that lead to published results must be archived and published in a trusted repository. Beyond policy compliance, publishing research data increases transparency, reproducibility, and the visibility and impact of your work.

Did you know?

Zenodo is derived from Zenodotus, the first librarian of the Library of Alexandria and father of the first recorded use of metadata

docs.title: Why use Zenodo?
docs.text:
• Free — no cost for uploading datasets up to 50 GB; multiple datasets can be uploaded with no size limit on communities.
  • Easy to use — intuitive interface with drag-and-drop file upload.
  • Accepts many formats — datasets, software, publications, posters, presentations, images, videos, and interactive materials.
  • DOI — every published record receives a DOI, making your data citable and findable.
  • Long-term preservation — data is stored in the trusted CERN data centre.
  • Increases visibility — widely known in the research community; data is searchable worldwide.
  • Complies with funder requirements — trusted by many funders and publishers as a reliable repository.
  • Supports open science — promotes transparency and reusability; supported by OpenAIRE.
  • Versioning — datasets can be updated as new versions.
  • GitHub integration — synchronise with a GitHub repository to preserve specific versions of your work.

docs.title: 1. Upload your data files
docs.text:
Log in to Zenodo and select New Upload to create a new draft record. Drag and drop your files into the upload box, or use the file browser.

When uploading, make sure your record includes:

  • Your data files — the datasets, scripts, or other outputs you want to archive
  • A README file — a plain text file (.md or .txt) describing the content of your uploaded files. Include it inside your ZIP archive or upload it as a separate file alongside your data.

README template and tips

Not sure what to include in your README? See the README section in our GEMs for recommended templates and examples to get inspired.

You cannot modify files after publishing

Once a record is published, you cannot add, remove, or modify data files — only metadata can be edited directly. To change files, you must create a new version, which generates a new DOI linked to the previous one. See Zenodo — How to manage versions.

docs.title: 2. Complete the metadata form
docs.text:
After uploading your files, complete the metadata form to describe your dataset. Good metadata ensures your dataset is findable, citable, and reusable.

The metadata fields are grouped into three categories — Basic (mandatory), Recommended, and Other (optional). Follow our dedicated best practice guide for step-by-step guidance on each field:

What next?

Files uploaded and metadata complete? Continue to Publishing to run pre-publishing checks and submit your record for publication on Zenodo.

docs.title: 1. Basic Information
docs.text:
Basic Information

Definition: Minimum description of the data package — visible once published. Type: Mandatory — complete all fields.

docs.title: Digital Object Identifier — Mandatory
docs.text:
• Reserve a DOI before publishing by clicking Get a DOI now! — the DOI is registered only when the record is published.
  • If you select Yes, do not provide a DOI linked to a journal article. Instead, add the article DOI in the Related works field.

docs.title: Resource Type — Mandatory
docs.text:
• Select Dataset for data files (e.g. CSV, XLS) and for data that includes scripts.
  • Select Software when publishing a software package or a specific version of a code repository.

docs.title: Title — Mandatory
docs.text:
• Provide a title that reflects the content of the data. The title is used in citations and for discovery.
  • Keep it concise. Use Add additional title/subtitle for very long titles.
  • A good format for datasets: "Dataset for [Title of your article]"
  • Avoid special characters (e.g. # % & @).

docs.title: Publication Date — Mandatory
docs.text:
• Defaults to the date the draft was created. Can be modified.
  • Use ISO format: YYYY-MM-DD.

docs.title: Creator — Mandatory
docs.text:
• A Creator is an author of the dataset and is included in the citation.
  • Search by ORCID to auto-populate name and affiliation.
  • It is highly recommended to provide an ORCID and a ROR affiliation for each Creator. The affiliation field is auto-completed from the ROR database.

docs.title: Description — Mandatory
docs.text:
• Provide a paragraph or short summary describing your dataset — it appears under the title once published.
  • Do not copy the abstract of your article — the Description should specifically describe the dataset.
  • The Description is not a substitute for a README file: the Description gives a general summary; the README describes the content of individual files.

A good example

See a good Description example from an A-LIFE researcher: Zenodo dataset.

docs.title: Licence — Mandatory
docs.text:
• A licence is required for others to reuse your data. By default, CC BY 4.0 is applied.
  • For datasets, see How do I licence my research data?.
  • For software, see Choose a Licence.
  • For an overview of common licences, see our GEMs — Licences page.

docs.title: Copyright — Recommended
docs.text: • A copyright statement describing ownership of the uploaded resource. By default: Copyright © (2025) The Authors.

docs.title: 2. Recommended Information
docs.text:
Recommended Information

Definition: Not strictly required to publish, but highly recommended for a complete and well-documented record. Type: Recommended

docs.title: Contributors — Optional
docs.text:
• Add Contributors in the same way as Creators — they are not included in the citation.
  • Do not add a person as a Contributor if they are already listed as a Creator.
  • Assign a Role (e.g. Supervisor, Contact person, Sponsor) — equivalent to someone you would include in manuscript Acknowledgements.

docs.title: Keywords and Subjects — Optional but highly recommended
docs.text:
• Keywords are free-form text; Subjects are from controlled vocabularies (e.g. Medical Subject Headings — MeSH).
  • Press Enter or click Add after each term to create separate tags — do not enter all terms as one string.
  • Check if your term is already in the European Science Vocabulary (EuroSciVoc) — shown as EuroSciVoc in the dropdown.
Selecting keywords and subjects from standard vocabularies

docs.title: Languages — Optional
docs.text: • More than one language can be selected.

docs.title: Dates — Optional
docs.text:
• Add specific date types beyond the publication date (e.g. submission or acceptance dates for preprints).
  • Use ISO format: YYYY-MM-DD.

docs.title: Version — Recommended
docs.text:
• For a first publication, use 1.0.0.
  • Increment the version number for each subsequent update (e.g. 1.1.0 follows 1.0.0).

Semantic versioning

See Introduction to semantic versioning for guidance on versioning datasets and software.

docs.title: Publisher — Optional
docs.text: • The Publisher appears in the citation. Zenodo is the default and will be visible in your record's citation. You may replace it with your institution's name.

docs.title: 3. Other Information
docs.text:
Other Information

Definition: Additional contextual information. Not mandatory, but recommended if the information exists. Type: Optional

docs.title: Funding — Optional but recommended
docs.text:
• Provide funding information for awards and grants associated with your research.
  • Standard award/grant: click + Add.
  • Custom award/grant: click + Add Custom — the funder must be registered in ROR.
  • More than one funding source can be added.

docs.title: Related works — Optional but highly recommended
docs.text:
• Use this field to cross-link your dataset with related publications, datasets, or other resources.
  • Mandatory sub-fields: Relation type, Identifier, and Scheme.
  • The most common relation type for datasets is Is Supplement To (links your dataset to a related article).
  • See the full list of DataCite Relation Types.

docs.title: References — Optional
docs.text: • Prefer using Related works to cross-link resources rather than this field.

docs.title: Software — Optional
docs.text:
• Relevant for Software resource types. Sub-fields: Repository URL, Programming language, and Repository status (e.g. Active).

Using GitHub with Zenodo?

Zenodo integrates with GitHub to automatically archive repository versions. See Referencing content on GitHub and Zenodo GitHub and Software.

docs.title: Publishing information — Optional
docs.text: • Relevant for manuscripts uploaded to Zenodo. Fields include Journal, Book, etc.

docs.title: Conference — Optional
docs.text: • Relevant for conference-related outputs (posters, presentations). Include the conference name and location.

docs.title: Domain specific fields — Optional
docs.text:
• Include domain-specific metadata where applicable.

What next?

Metadata complete! Continue to Step 3 — Publishing in Zenodo to run pre-publishing checks and submit your record.

  1. GitHub Docs — Referencing and citing content: https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/archiving-a-github-repository/referencing-and-citing-content ↩

  2. Zenodo Documentation — GitHub and Software: https://help.zenodo.org/docs/github/ ↩

docs.title: Documenting a Zenodo Package
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Documenting a Zenodo Package page, part of Zenodo → Other Tools in the A-LIFE RDM collection.

Before archiving in Zenodo, good documentation makes your dataset findable, citable, and reusable. This page covers:

  • Metadata — the structured fields you will fill in during archiving
  • README — the human-readable file you prepare before uploading

Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-06-27 — Version: 0.1.0

docs.title: Two layers of documentation
docs.text:
A well-documented Zenodo package has two complementary layers:

  • Metadata — structured fields (title, creators, description, licence, resource type, etc.) that you fill in directly in the Zenodo interface when creating a record. Metadata is machine-readable, feeds search engines and data catalogues, and makes your dataset findable and citable. Some fields are mandatory; others are strongly recommended.
  • README — a plain text file that you write and include inside your uploaded files (or ZIP archive). It is human-readable and describes the content of the files, how the data was collected, and how to use it. The README is not enforced by Zenodo, but it is strongly recommended and required by the A-LIFE checklist before archiving.

Metadata answers "what is this dataset?" for search engines and catalogues. The README answers "what is in these files?" for the person who downloads them.

docs.title: 1. Metadata
docs.text:
When you create a new upload in Zenodo, you fill in a metadata form as part of the archiving process. The form includes three categories of fields: Basic (mandatory), Recommended, and Other (optional).

Getting the metadata right before you start archiving will speed up the process and ensure your dataset is properly described from the moment of publication.

Key things to prepare in advance:

  • Title — a clear, descriptive title for the dataset (not just "data")
  • Creators — names, affiliations, and ORCID identifiers for all contributors
  • Description — a concise summary of what the dataset contains and what research it supports; you can copy the key content from your README
  • Resource type — choose the type that best fits (dataset, software, poster, etc.)
  • Licence — decide which licence applies to your data before uploading; check with your data steward if unsure
  • Related publications — link your dataset to any associated article using its DOI

For step-by-step guidance on every field in the Zenodo metadata form, follow our dedicated best practice guide:

BP — Zenodo — Metadata Form

docs.title: 2. README
docs.text:
A README is a plain text file (.md or .txt) that describes the content of your dataset. Include it inside your ZIP archive or upload it as a separate file alongside your data files.

What a good Zenodo README should cover:

  • A short description of the dataset and what research question or publication it supports
  • A list of the files or folders included, with a brief description of each
  • Information about how the data was collected, generated, or processed
  • Software, tools, or dependencies needed to open or work with the files
  • Licence information
  • Contact details

Tip

Copy the key description from your README into the Zenodo Description field when filling in the metadata form — this ensures the content is visible on the dataset landing page without requiring a download.

README template and tips

See the README section in our GEMs for a ready-to-use template and examples.

What next?

Metadata prepared and README ready? Continue to Archiving in Zenodo to upload your files and complete the metadata form in Zenodo.

docs.title: Organise your Data
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Organise your Data page, part of Zenodo → Other Tools in the A-LIFE RDM collection.

This page provides guidance on how to prepare and organise your data before archiving in Zenodo:

  • How Zenodo organises data
  • Why organise before uploading
  • Before you upload

Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-06-26 — Version: 0.1.0

docs.title: What does a Zenodo record need?
docs.text:
Each record you publish in Zenodo requires the following:

Requirement Description Data files The files you want to archive and publish — datasets, software, documents, or other outputs Metadata Title, creators, description, resource type, licence, and more — describes your dataset README file Highly recommended — describes the content of your uploaded files; include it inside your ZIP or as a separate file DOI Automatically assigned at publication — makes your dataset citable and permanently findable

docs.title: 1. How Zenodo organises data
docs.text:
In Zenodo, each record corresponds to one published dataset. A record contains:

  • The data files you upload (individual files or a ZIP archive)
  • The metadata describing your dataset (title, creators, description, licence, etc.)
  • A DOI assigned at the time of publication

Unlike a shared drive or folder structure, Zenodo does not have a nested folder hierarchy — each record is a flat collection of files under a single DOI. If you want to publish separate datasets (e.g. two experiments), you create two separate records.

docs.title: 2. Why organise before uploading
docs.text:
Once a record is published in Zenodo, not everything can be changed in the same way:

  • Metadata (title, creators, description, licence, etc.) — can be edited directly at any time, without creating a new version.
  • Data files (adding, removing, or modifying files) — requires creating a new version of the record. Each new version gets its own DOI, which is automatically linked to all previous versions — so existing citations still work. But ideally, you want to get it right the first time.

Taking a few minutes to organise your data before uploading will save you from having to republish. Good organisation also ensures that:

  • Others can understand and reuse your data without needing to contact you
  • Your dataset complies with FAIR data principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable)
  • Your metadata accurately describes what is in the files

Need guidance on organising research data?

See the BP — RDM — Organising Data guide for general best practices on folder structures and file naming conventions.

docs.title: 3. Before you upload
docs.text:
• 1. Decide what to publish Include only the data needed to reproduce or understand your results — not raw instrument exports or intermediate files unless needed. If publishing data linked to a paper, focus on what supports the paper's conclusions.

  • 2. Use clear, consistent file names Avoid spaces and special characters (use _ or - instead). Use descriptive names: experiment1_results_2025.csv is better than data_final_v3.csv.

  • 3. Package files correctly If you have more than ~20 files, ZIP them into a single archive before uploading. Remove hidden files (e.g. .DS_Store, __MACOSX) from ZIP archives. Maximum: 100 files per record, 50 GB per record.

  • 4. Prepare a README Include a README file in plain text format (.md or .txt) describing the content of your uploaded files. Copy the key content into the Zenodo Description field so it is visible on the landing page.

  • 5. Check your data classification Confirm whether your data is Open, Restricted, or not suitable for public sharing. If your data contains sensitive or personal information, do not upload it to Zenodo without first consulting your data steward.

README template and tips

See the README section in our GEMs for recommended templates and examples to get inspired.

What next?

Data organised and ready? Continue to Archiving in Zenodo to upload your files and complete the metadata form.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Publishing page, part of Zenodo → Other Tools in the A-LIFE RDM collection.

This document covers the final steps before publishing your dataset in Zenodo:

  • Pre-publishing checks
  • How to publish your data in Zenodo

Supporting materials: GEMs, FAQs Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-02-23 — Version: 0.6.0

docs.title: 1. Pre-publishing checks
docs.text:
Complete these checks before submitting for publication

We strongly recommend going through each check below before publishing — it helps you catch errors and ensures your dataset meets quality standards.

docs.title: 1a. Draft Preview
docs.text:
Before publishing the dataset, it is highly recommended to select the Preview option of the draft. It is on the side right side bar of the interface.

Draft preview option

In the Preview option, you are able to view how the record will look like once it is published. This is always highly recommended to do as you will be able to also spot errors.

Preview Display Record View

docs.title: 1b. Share Access
docs.text:
Zenodo also provides the possibility to Share your draft with others before submitting.

Share the data record

It is possible to add Zenodo users and invite people by sending an invitation.

Add a member

This is useful for collaborating in the same draft before submitting and checking with your collaborators if everything provided is correct. It is requested to provide the type of Access for the new person added.

Manage user accessibility

docs.title: 1c. Visibility
docs.text:
Zenodo provides only two options for data Accessibility: Open and Restricted.

  • Open allows all the metadata and all the data published to be public, thus visible and accessible to everyone. This includes also the option to download the data files.
Open Accessibility
  • For the Restricted option, only the metadta information will be visible while the data files can only be accessed by users specified in the permissions.
Restricted option

docs.title: 1d. Community
docs.text:
Zenodo provides the possibility to submit the dataset to a Community. This option can be done by "Select a Community"option.

Select a community option

There is then a selection of communities that you can pick from. Submit your dataset record for inclusion in a Community from the list. The Community curators are responsible for curating the dataset record and finally accept/decline the record into the Community. More than one Community can be selected.

Select a community from the list

Submitting your record to a Community offers several advantages -- such as increasing the visibility and impact of your research. It improves findability, accessibility, and reusability of your dataset, and can also lead to institutional recognition and metadata improvement.

Communities in Zenodo

Read more about how to submit to a Community and how to create a Community in Zenodo submit to community1.

docs.title: 2. How to publish your data in Zenodo
docs.text:
You can only delete an unpublished record. Published records cannot be deleted except under special circumstances. You can save the dataset draft and review it before finally clicking the "Publish" button to make it publicly accessible. Make sure you have followed the Visibility option check correctly for the data files access.

Publish record

What can you change after publishing?

Once your record is published, not everything works the same way:

  • Metadata (title, creators, description, licence, etc.) — can be edited directly at any time without creating a new version.
  • Data files (adding, removing, or modifying files) — requires creating a new version of the record. This generates a new DOI for the updated version.

New versions are linked to all previous versions — so if someone has cited or saved an earlier DOI, it still works and points to that specific version. Zenodo also always provides a link to the most recent version, so users can find the latest update.

See Zenodo — How to manage versions2 for step-by-step instructions.

Your dataset is now live in Zenodo!

Congratulations — your dataset has a permanent DOI and is now openly available, citable, and searchable worldwide. You have made your research reusable for others!

Share your DOI with us at data@aimms.vu.nl — we would love to feature it as an example in our growing documentation.

Further reading

Zenodo Help Documentation Zenodo — Submit to a Community Zenodo — How to manage versions

  1. Zenodo | Documentation — Submit to community: https://help.zenodo.org/docs/share/submit-to-community/ ↩

  2. Zenodo | Documentation — Manage versions: https://help.zenodo.org/docs/deposit/manage-versions/ ↩

docs.title: Getting Started with Zenodo
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Getting Started page, part of Zenodo → Other Tools in the A-LIFE RDM collection.

This document covers the first steps for using Zenodo:

  • Pre-Requirements — Sign up
  • Login
  • Upload Data
  • Best Practices for a good data file upload

Supporting materials: GEMs, FAQs Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-02-19 — Version: 0.6.0

docs.title: 1. Pre-Requirements — Sign up
docs.text:
Already have a Zenodo account?

If you already have an account, skip to 2. Login.

docs.title: 1a. Register
docs.text:
To use Zenodo, you need a Zenodo account. Register here using your email address.

Use a personal email address

It is recommended to register with a personal email address rather than your institutional one — you may change institutions and lose access to your institutional account.

docs.title: 1b. Link your Accounts
docs.text:
You can connect other accounts to your Zenodo account by selecting Settings → Linked accounts from the dropdown beside your email address. Available options are ORCID, GitHub, and OpenAIRE.

Connecting accounts to Zenodo

Recommendation

It is highly recommended to link your ORCID. Once linked, you can use it to log in and your author information will be auto-populated in new records.

docs.title: 2. Login
docs.text: Log in at https://zenodo.org using your email, ORCID, or GitHub credentials (if linked). After login, select New Upload to start a new dataset record.

docs.title: 3. Upload Data
docs.text:
The New Upload option creates a new draft record. You will then see the Upload your files option — drag and drop files directly into the upload box, or use the file browser.

Initiating a New Upload in Zenodo

Uploading data files in the new record

You can fill in metadata before uploading

There is no required order — you can complete the metadata fields before uploading your files. Your record stays as a Draft until you decide to publish.

Always include a README

Include a README file as part of your dataset. See the Essentials — README section for templates and guidance.

docs.title: 4. Best Practices for a good data file upload
docs.text:
1. Check the number of files and size

  • Maximum 100 files per dataset record.
  • Maximum 50 GB per dataset.
  • For larger uploads, see How to request a quota increase.

2. Package files in a ZIP archive

  • When uploading more than 20 files, it is recommended to ZIP your folder first.

3. Check file names and formats

  • Remove hidden files (e.g. .DS_Store, __MACOSX) from ZIP archives before uploading.

4. Include your README file

  • Include a README that describes the content of your uploaded files.
  • Include the README inside the ZIP file, or upload it separately alongside other files.
  • Repeat the key README content in the Zenodo Description field so it is visible on the record landing page.
  • Provide the README in plain text format (.md or .txt) — avoid .docx.

5. Select your preview file

  • The preview file is displayed when someone accesses the DOI. By default, it follows alphanumerical order.
  • Change the preview file by checking the Preview checkbox in the file list.
  • If uploading individual files (not a ZIP), set the README as the preview file.

Preview file selection

6. Check your data classification

  • If your data is set to Open, make sure you are not accidentally sharing sensitive data.
  • If unsure, check with your data management team before publishing.

You cannot modify data files after publishing

Once a record is published, you cannot add, remove, or modify data files. To make changes, you must create a new version of the record. See Zenodo — How to manage versions.

What next?

Account set up and ready to go! Continue to Step 2 — Organise your Data to prepare your files before uploading.

docs.title: VU Storage Tools
docs.text:
Overview

This is the VU Storage Tools section, part of the Tools collection. It covers VU-supported storage solutions and helps you choose the right one for your research data.

Supporting materials: GEMs — Resources — FAQs Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-06-22 — Version: 0.8.0

docs.title: Introduction — Choosing the right VU Storage Tool
docs.text:
As a researcher, you will often face the question: "Where should I store my files?". The best answer depends on several factors. This page is structured into the following sections:

  1. Documentation to VU storage Tools
  2. What to consider when choosing a storage solution
  3. Where to find more information

The VU provides multiple storage solutions, each suited for different data types, workflows, and access requirements. You may need a combination at different stages of your project.

docs.title: 1. Documentation
docs.text:
Please select which VU Storage Solution you would like to look into more detail:

Yoda — Active Storage Research Drive

docs.title: 2. What to consider when choosing a storage solution
docs.text:
Research projects often involve multiple data collections, each with unique storage requirements. For this reason, you need to consider the following when selecting a storage solution:

Checklist for selecting a storage solution

  • Data volume — How much data do you need to store, daily or over the entire project?
  • Purpose
    • Why do you want to put the data on a new storage solution?
    • Is your data too large for your laptop?
    • Do you need secure storage for your project?
    • Do you need to back up your data? Share it, or archive your date?
  • Access frequency — Also known as the data temperature, how often will you need to access or modify your data?
    • Hot data — constantly accessed, analysed, and modified, typical of data being processed/generated/explored (active data)
    • Cool data — Is less likely to be changing but needs to be accessible - typical of measurement data that needs to be available for further analysis.
    • Frozen data — read-only, preserved for the long term (archived data)
  • Storage duration — For how long do you need to store the data?
  • Usage — How do you work or interact with the data? For example, Excel, Python/R scripts, instruments
  • Collaboration — Are you working on the data by yourseful or you need to share it with other researchers?
  • Sharing scope — Are collaborators within VU, external, or both?
  • Data sensitivity — For example, is it obtained from, or about, a human subject: that falls under the GDPR/AVG legislation, or more sensitive patient/medical data?
  • Budget - Does your project include, or do you have, a budget for storing/archiving this data?

docs.title: 3. Where to find more information
docs.text: Finding the right storage solution can be challenging, as information is often fragmented across different resources. While the VU does provide some information, research groups, departments and disciplines can all also have their own "in-house" storage. Here are some pointers to finding the best storage for your data:

docs.title: 3a. Ask your network
docs.text: Ask your colleagues in your research group and research section what they use, usually the practical experience is often the fastest guide.

docs.title: 3b. Check the VU Storage Finder
docs.text:
Try the VU Data Storage Finder. This interactive tool gives an overview of available options at the VU — even browsing the tiles without using the filters is informative.

Figure 1: VU Storage Finder (version accessed on 2026-06-22)

docs.title: 3c. Contact RDM A-LIFE support
docs.text:
Contact your local RDM support for more information and the design of custom storage solutions:

  • Data Steward: Brett Olivier — data@aimms.vu.nl
  • A-LIFE Data Specialist: Irene Martorelli — i.martorelli@vu.nl

docs.text:

docs.text:

    Access your Research Drive project space directly via the web interface.

  • Request Storage Space

    Request a Research Drive project space via VU research data support.

docs.title: What is Research Drive?
docs.text:
Research Drive is a cloud-based storage service provided by SURF1, recommended at the VU for the active storage of research data during a project.

  1. It is primarily designed for the active storage of "hot" and "warm" research data — data that is active during a research project, before publication, or shared across multiple projects.
  2. RD allows for very fine-grained sharing, making it one of the more suitable tools for collaboration between researchers both inside and outside the VU.
  3. It is a project-based cloud storage hosted by SURF — data is linked to a project, not to a specific person (unlike OneDrive). You can store and share data via browser and synchronise with various devices.
  4. RD is suitable for personal and sensitive data with classification medium. For high or above, contact a Privacy Champion or use the VU Data Storage Finder.
  5. While RD supports flexible storage for larger amounts of data, projects exceeding 500 GB incur costs. See the VU Storage Cost Model for more details.

docs.title: Why use Research Drive?
docs.text:
• User-friendly — intuitive interface for creating, managing, and moving files and folders.
  • Ideal for collaboration — fine-grained, folder-based sharing with multiple users inside and outside the VU.
  • Secure — MFA for both login and folder sharing.
  • Institutionally supported — supported by VU University Library (UB) and the RDM support desk.
  • Multiple access options — accessible via web browser, synchronisation client, or any WebDAV-capable client.
  • Familiar interface — if you have used SURFDrive before, Research Drive will feel very familiar.

New to Research Drive?

If you have never used Research Drive before, you must start with Step 1 — Getting Started to request access before you can do anything else.

docs.title: Research Drive Workflow
docs.text: Follow these steps to get started with Research Drive and manage your data throughout your project.

docs.title: Step 1 — Getting Started
docs.text:
Before using Research Drive, you need to request a project storage space. Our documentation provides guidance on how to request access and get started:

Getting Started with Research Drive

docs.title: Step 2 — Organise your Space
docs.text:
Before uploading data, it is worth thinking about how to structure your project folder. A clear folder hierarchy makes sharing and access management much easier, and will save effort when data is later moved to Yoda for archiving.

Organise your Research Drive Space

docs.title: Step 3 — Access and Transfer Data
docs.text:
Once your space is organised, you can start uploading and managing your data. Research Drive can be accessed via the web interface, a sync client, or a WebDAV connection.

Transferring Data

docs.title: Step 4 — Manage Group Members
docs.text:
Research Drive allows fine-grained sharing at the folder level, making it easy to collaborate with researchers inside and outside the VU.

Manage Group Members

docs.title: Step 5 — Archiving and Publishing your Data
docs.text:
Research Drive is not an archive or a publishing platform

Research Drive is designed for active (warm) storage only. Data stored here is not preserved for the long term, does not receive a persistent identifier (DOI), and cannot be published directly. Once your project is complete, you must move your data to a dedicated archiving and publishing platform.

When your project is complete and your files are finalised, we recommend transferring your data to a dedicated archiving and publishing platform. Depending on your use case and dataset, we recommend the following VU-supported tools:

  • Yoda — for long-term archiving and optional publication of research data. You can transfer data directly from Research Drive to your Yoda Research Space (we recommend Cyberduck for this). Follow our documentation for archiving and publishing in Yoda:

Transferring Data to Yoda Archiving in Yoda Publishing in Yoda

  • Zenodo — a free, open-access repository suitable for publishing datasets, software, and other research outputs. Follow our documentation for publishing in Zenodo:

Publishing in Zenodo

docs.text:
For questions or support, contact your local RDM team:

  • A-LIFE Data Steward: Brett Olivier — data@aimms.vu.nl

docs.text:
Overview

This is the Manage Group Members page, part of Research Drive → VU Tools in the A-LIFE RDM collection.

This page covers how to share your Research Drive project space with collaborators, set permissions, and manage group access.

  • Sharing your project folder

docs.title: :folder_open: 1. Sharing your project folder
docs.text:
Once your Research Drive project space is set up, you can share it with collaborators inside and outside the VU. Sharing in Research Drive works at the folder level — you control who has access to each folder and what they can do with it.

To share a folder:

  1. Go to the main folder overview in your Research Drive space.
  2. Click the ... (three dots) next to the folder name.
  3. Click Details.
  4. In the Activities tab, you can see who the folder is already shared with.
  5. In the Sharing tab, you have options to share with Users, Groups, or Federated users (external institutions).
  6. Type a name — you can use either a VU name or VUID.

Further reading

SURF — How to upload or download files

docs.title: 2. Invite a new user
docs.text:
As the project owner or group admin, you can invite new users — both internal (VU) and external — to your Research Drive space.

How it works:

  1. Go to the Dashboard and find the Invite user or Invitation App.
  2. Fill in the recipient's email address and send the invitation.
  3. The invited person receives an email with a unique, one-time link.
  4. Clicking the link guides them to create a Research Drive account (if they do not have one) or log in with existing credentials.
  5. Once they accept and register, they become a member of your group with the permissions you assigned.

Internal vs external users

  • Internal VU users may log in with their existing institutional credentials but still receive an invite email.
  • External users always receive a link to set up a Research Drive account.

Further reading

SURF — Invite a new user

docs.title: 3. Roles and permissions
docs.text:
When sharing a folder, you can assign different permission levels by clicking the wheel icon next to the user's name:

Permission Description Share User can share the folder with others (does not automatically include edit rights) Edit User can edit files — automatically includes Create, Change, and Delete Create User can add new files and folders Change User can modify existing files Delete User can delete files and folders

Check permissions carefully

Assigning Edit automatically grants Create, Change, and Delete. Assigning Share alone does not grant edit rights — these must be set separately.

Further reading

SURF — Roles and permissions SURF — Set permissions when sharing files and folders

docs.title: 4. Managing groups
docs.text:
For projects involving multiple collaborators, using custom groups is the recommended approach. Groups allow you to manage access for multiple users at once and assign different permission levels to different folders.

  • Create a personal group via your Personal Settings → Custom Groups.
  • Share your project folder with the group rather than individual users.
  • Manage member roles (member, moderator, admin) at the group level.

Further reading

SURF — Groups

What next?

Once your collaborators have access, continue to Step 5 — Archiving and Publishing your Data.

docs.title: How Research Drive is structured
docs.text:
Research Drive is a project-based cloud storage. When your space is created, you get a single root folder linked to your project, prefixed with your faculty code (e.g. BETA_project-name).

Within your project space you can create your own folder structure, share specific folders with collaborators, and manage access at the folder level.

Research Drive is designed for active storage — it is not an archiving solution. When your project is complete, your data should be moved to Yoda or another archiving platform.

docs.title: Why organise before uploading
docs.text:
Reorganising data after uploading to Research Drive is possible but can quickly become cumbersome, especially when collaborators already have access to your folders. We recommend setting up your structure before you start:

  • Folder structure determines sharing — sharing in Research Drive works at the folder level, so a well-structured folder hierarchy makes access management much easier.
  • Consistent naming saves time — when data is later moved to Yoda for archiving, a clean and consistent naming convention avoids extra work at that stage.
  • Avoid duplicates — moving and copying large files between folders without a clear structure can quickly lead to duplicate files.

docs.title: Before you upload

docs.title: What is Yoda?
docs.text:
Yoda is a research data management platform recommended at the VU that supports the entire research cycle — from the safe storage and sharing of active research data, to archiving and publishing completed datasets.

In practice, Yoda serves two key functions in the research data lifecycle:

  • Active storage — a secure cloud space for storing and sharing data during your project.
  • Archiving & publishing — finalised datasets are submitted to the Vault, a read-only long-term storage space, where they can optionally be published and assigned a persistent identifier (DOI).

docs.title: Yoda Workflow

Follow these steps in order to get started with Yoda and take your data from the active storage to publication.

New to Yoda?

This page covers:

docs.title: What is archiving in Yoda?
docs.text:
In Yoda, archiving and publishing are two distinct steps — unlike some repositories such as Zenodo, where both happen simultaneously when you publish a record:

  • Archiving — submitting a data package to the Vault creates a read-only, long-term copy of your folder. Once accepted into the Vault, a data package cannot be changed or deleted. The data is securely preserved but not publicly accessible.
  • Publishing — a subsequent, optional step that makes your data (or its metadata) publicly visible and assigns a DOI.

According to the VU Research Data and Software Management Policy (2024)1 (NL), archived data and software must contain everything that supports the published result, including appropriate documentation and metadata, so that the research process is transparent and verifiable.

Archiving in Yoda follows a review process:

  1. You fill in the Yoda Metadata Form for the folder you want to archive.
  2. You submit the folder as a data package to the Vault.
  3. A data manager reviews the submission for completeness and compliance before a copy is moved to the Vault — they will either approve it or request changes.
  4. Once approved, the data package is stored as a read-only copy in the Vault and visible under the Vault tab.

You can only publish after archiving — archiving alone does not assign a DOI

In Yoda, publication is only possible for data packages that have already been archived in the Vault. Archiving always comes first — but archiving alone does not make your data public or assign a DOI. A DOI is only assigned when you proceed to the publishing step.

When should you archive?

It is strongly recommended to archive at the end of the research project or when an article is published that relies on the data as its source.2

docs.title: 1. Pre-checks before submitting to the Vault
docs.text:
Before submitting, make sure you have completed the Metadata and Documenting Data steps, then go through the checklist below.

Checklist before submitting in the vault

  • 1. The metadata form is complete

  • Make sure all required fields in the Yoda Metadata Form are filled in and correspond to the folder you want to archive. Follow the steps in the Accessing and Filling the Metadata Form section of the Metadata and Documentation page.

  • 2. The data package folder contains a README file

  • Include a README file documenting the content of the files and aligning with the metadata. See the GEMs — README for templates and tips.

  • 3. The licence is adequate and aligns with your Data Package Access

  • If Restricted or Closed is selected, you are responsible for adding a custom licence.txt file. See licence guidance.

  • 4. Your folder structure is well-organised and file names are clear

  • A consistent structure and descriptive file names make your dataset easier to review and reuse. See Organise your Data.

  • 5. No sensitive data is included in open files

  • If your data is labelled Open, verify that no identifiable or sensitive information is included in any of the files.

  • 6. Your collaborators have checked the submission

  • Before submitting, confirm with collaborators that everything in the folder is correct and ready for archiving.

  • 7. Check for typos and broken links

  • Review names, titles, and metadata fields for typos. Verify that any URLs (DOIs, repository links) resolve correctly.

docs.title: 2. Submitting to the Vault
docs.text:
Once you have gone through the checklist and everything is in place, go to your Research Space in Yoda, navigate to Actions and click the Submit button.

Submit will send the data package for review to the Institutional data manager. You will be notified by email once it is approved or when changes need to be made for approval.

When the data package is approved, the data folder will be visible in the Vault, the Yoda archive space.

Important — do not forget to clean up your Research Space!

When your data package is accepted into the Vault, a copy of the folder is placed there — the original folder in your Research Space is not removed automatically.

After archiving, go back to your Research Space and delete the folder you just archived. Do not delete any other folders — only the one that is now safely stored in the Vault.

What next?

Your data package has been submitted for archiving! Once approved, it will be visible in the Vault.

Are you ready to also publish your dataset? Follow Step 6 — Publishing in Yoda to make your data publicly available and receive a DOI!

docs.title: Metadata Form and README
docs.text:
In Yoda, documentation before archiving consists of two elements:

  • The Metadata Form — mandatory. Yoda will not let you submit a data package to the Vault without a completed metadata form. It is a structured set of fields (title, creators, licence, description, etc.) attached to each folder in your Research Space. The metadata is also used when publishing — it appears in data catalogues such as DataCite. Yoda uses the DataCite metadata standard, which ensures interoperability with international research data registries.
  • A README file — highly recommended. A plain text file that lives inside your data package folder, describing the content of the files for anyone who downloads or accesses the data. It is not enforced by Yoda, but is required by the A-LIFE checklist before submitting.

docs.title: 1. Accessing the Yoda Metadata Form
docs.text:
Warning

You can only access your project space in Yoda if you have first requested storage space and been granted access. Follow the instructions in Getting Started with Yoda.

  1. Login to the VU Yoda Portal — https://portal.yoda.vu.nl For login instructions see Getting Started with Yoda.

  2. Go to your Research Space Once logged in, select Research to access your active project space in Yoda.

  3. Access the Metadata form In the Research portal you will see your project folders. Click the Metadata box on the folder you want to archive. The Metadata form is found in the top left corner of the interface of your Research Space. Each project folder has its own metadata form. If a subfolder's form is not filled in, it inherits the metadata of the parent folder.

  4. Complete the Metadata form You are now able to fill in the metadata fields for your project folder.

Warning

Please be aware that some of the field names have been recently renamed. If you have already metadata forms filled in for projects in Yoda that you have not recently accessed, you will have the following message (Last updated: 2025-07-02):

Further reading — Understanding the Yoda Metadata Schema

VU RDM — Yoda Metadata Schema and Reuse — learn how metadata fields are structured, how they map to the DataCite standard, and how metadata can be reused across folders.

docs.title: 2. Completing the Metadata Form
docs.text:
The Yoda Metadata Form contains a number of required and recommended fields. Completing them carefully ensures a smoother review and better discoverability when your dataset is published.

For detailed guidance on each metadata field, follow our guide:

Best Practices — Completing the Yoda Metadata Form

docs.title: 3. Documenting your Data
docs.text: We explicitly recommend including a README file in your Yoda data package folder before archiving. A README is a plain text file (.md or .txt) that describes the content of your files for anyone who downloads or accesses the dataset — now or in the future.

docs.title: What to include in your README
docs.text:
At a minimum, your README should include information about the dataset and its creators:

  • Dataset title and description — what the dataset contains and what research question or publication it supports
  • Authors and affiliations — names, institutions, and ORCID identifiers where available
  • Licence — the licence that applies to the data (especially important for Restricted or Closed packages)
  • Contact — name and email address for questions about the dataset

And recommended information about the content of the data package:

  • File list — a list of all files and folders in the data package with a short description of each
  • File and column descriptions — for tabular data, describe the column headers, units, and any coded values or abbreviations used
  • Data collection and processing methods — how the data was generated, collected, or processed, including instruments, software, or experimental conditions

Unlike the metadata form, which feeds the Yoda system and data catalogues, the README is human-readable documentation that lives inside your data package folder alongside your files. Most of the information you include in a README maps directly to fields in the Yoda Metadata Form — writing both together is a natural process.

A README is recommended in all folders independently of which tool is used for storage. For example, a README can be initially created in Research Drive to describe a folder during the active phase of your project — the same file can then be transferred without modification into Yoda when you archive your data package.

It is highly recommended to place the README file in the root folder of the data package you want to archive, so that it is directly visible and findable to anyone accessing the dataset.

README templates and further guidance

See the README section in our GEMs for a copy-paste template and practical tips.

Get inspired by your A-LIFE colleagues!

Not sure where to start? A great way to get inspired is to look at what your A-LIFE colleagues have done! The datasets below are published by A-LIFE researchers and archived in Yoda — each includes a README you can browse directly in the Vault. Take a look at how they described their files and structured their documentation. Every research domain is different, so feel free to adapt what you see to your own workflow.

docs.title: Manage Group Members in Yoda
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Manage Group Members page, part of VU Tools → Yoda in the A-LIFE RDM collection.

This page explains how to manage access to your Yoda Research Space, including user roles and how to add both VU-affiliated and external collaborators:

  • Adding VU-affiliated users
  • Inviting external users

Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-06-27 — Version: 0.1.0

docs.title: Who manages the group?
docs.text:
When you submit the Request Yoda Space form, two roles are defined:

  • Project Manager — the head of the research project, responsible for the overall project
  • Project Owner — the person managing the data day-to-day (can be the same person as the Project Manager)

Both the Project Manager and the Project Owner are automatically granted Group Manager permissions in Yoda. This means they are the ones responsible for granting access to other members of the Research Space.

Two owners are better than one

It is strongly recommended to have at least two Group Managers per Research Space. This ensures that access management is not blocked if one person is unavailable, and reduces the risk of losing administrative control over the space.

Share with the minimum necessary

Only add members who genuinely need access to the Research Space — either to view the data or to contribute to it as required by the project. Limiting access reduces security risks and keeps the group manageable.

docs.title: 1. Adding VU-affiliated users
docs.text:
Members with a VU affiliation (VUnetID) can be added to your Yoda Research Space directly by a Group Manager — no invitation email is required. Once added, they can log in immediately via https://portal.yoda.vu.nl using their VU credentials.

VUnetID — your personal credentials for accessing all VU Amsterdam digital services. VU Amsterdam — VUnetID information

docs.title: Steps for adding a VU-affiliated member
docs.text:
1. Log in to the VU Yoda Portal — https://portal.yoda.vu.nl and go to your Research Space.

    Figure 1: Research Space in the Yoda Portal

  2. Browse to your project — click on the Research tab and select the project you want to manage. Click on the project name to open its folders.

  3. Open the Group Manager — click on "Go to group manager" to access the group management interface.

    Figure 2: Group Manager access

  4. Add a new member — enter the VU email address of the person you want to add, assign them a role, and confirm.

    Only Group Managers can add members

    Adding members to a Yoda project is only allowed by a Group Manager. If you do not have this role, contact your project's Group Manager to request access for new members.

    Figure 3: Adding a new group member

    You need to assign a role to the new member you would like to include.

    Figure 4: Selecting a role for the new group member

    The available roles are:

    Role Accessibility Description Viewer Read-only Can view and download files in the group Member Read / Write Can view, download, upload, modify, or delete files and folders in the group Manager Read / Write / Admin Can grant and revoke access rights for the group; can also view, download, upload, modify, or delete files and folders in the group

    Only Managers can add and remove members

    Only users with the Manager role can add or remove members from a Yoda group. If you do not have this role, contact your project's Manager to manage group access.

    The roles of existing members are visible via the icons displayed before their name in the Group Manager window. To change a member's role, click on their email address in the Group Manager window.

docs.title: Steps for the new member — accepting the invitation
docs.text:
Once added, the new member will receive an email from SURF Research Access Management (SRAM) with the subject line "Invitation to join collaboration yoda-research-[name-of-project]". They must follow the steps below to accept the invitation and access the Research Space.

Do not ignore the invitation email!

The invitation link is time-limited — if it is not accepted within the validity period, it will expire and a new invitation will need to be sent. Make sure to inform your new member to check their inbox (including spam) and act on the invitation promptly.

  1. Join the collaboration — click on the blue link found in the SURF invitation email to proceed to the collaboration join page.

    Figure 4: SURF invitation email — join collaboration link

  2. Accept the invitation — on the collaboration page, click the blue button "Log in to accept the invite".

    Figure 5: Accept the collaboration invitation

  3. Login via your institution — select Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam by clicking the grey box with the VU icon and log in with your VU credentials.

    Figure 6: Select Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam to log in

  4. Access the research data project — after logging in, click the blue button "Proceed to yoda-research-[name-of-project]" to enter the Research Space. From this point onwards you can log in directly via the Yoda portal.

    [screenshot to be added]

docs.title: 2. Inviting external users
docs.text: Collaborators without a VU affiliation need to be invited through a different process. External users will receive an invitation by email and must complete a registration step before they can access the Research Space.

docs.title: Steps for the new member — logging in without a VU affiliation
docs.text:
The steps for joining the collaboration and accepting the invitation are the same as for VU-affiliated users (steps 1–2 above). The difference is at the login step:

  1. Login via your institution — if your institute is included in the list of institutions using SRAM, you can select your institution name from the list, which will redirect you to your familiar institutional login page. If your institute is not part of the list, when you try to login you will see the following page:

    Figure: Login page shown when your institution is not part of the SRAM list

  2. Create an eduID if you do not have one — if your institution is not in the SRAM list, you can log in using eduID (NL).

    If you do not yet have an eduID, follow the instructions in the Manual: Create an eduID first, then return here to continue.

  3. Select eduID (NL) to log in — go back to the SRAM invitation link you received by email and select eduID (NL) from the list of login options. This option will be used every time you access the project via the Yoda portal.

    Figure: Selecting eduID (NL) from the SRAM login options

  4. Access the research data project — after logging in with your eduID, you will see the SRAM welcome screen. Click Proceed to accept the invitation and access the Yoda Research Space.

What next?

Group members set up? Continue to Metadata and Documentation to prepare your data package for archiving.

docs.title: Organise your Data
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Organising Data page, part of Yoda → Storage Tools in the A-LIFE RDM collection.

This page explains how Yoda is structured and why we recommend organising your data locally before transferring it. Follow our guide Best Practices for organising your data for support on directory structure, file naming and file versioning — this guide can be used for organising data for any tools and devices, including your desktop.

Supporting materials: Best Practices — Organising data Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-06-24 — Version: 0.1.0

docs.title: How Yoda is structured
docs.text:
Yoda has two main spaces:

  • Research Space — the active working area where you store and share data during your project.
  • Vault — the long-term archive. When you submit a folder from the Research Space to the Vault, it becomes a read-only data package. The folder structure and file names become part of the permanent record.

For a full overview of Yoda's features, see the VU Research Support Handbook — Yoda.

docs.title: Why organise before transferring
docs.text:
Yoda is a storage and archiving platform, not a file manager. We recommend organising your data locally before uploading for the following reasons:

  • Renaming inside Yoda is cumbersome — via WebDAV, renaming copies and deletes rather than truly renaming, which is slow for large datasets.
  • Sync tools will not recognise renames — tools like Cyberduck sync or Rclone treat a renamed file as a new file, uploading a duplicate and leaving the old name behind.1
  • Folder structure becomes your archive — the folder you submit to the Vault is your data package. Inconsistent naming carries over permanently into the archive and any published record.

docs.title: Before you transfer
docs.text:
Follow our general guide for support on directory structure, file naming and file versioning. It applies to any tool or device, not just Yoda.

Best Practices — Organising data

What next?

Once your data is organised, continue to Step 3 — Transfer Data in Yoda.

  1. WebDAV rename behaviour: RFC 4918 — HTTP Extensions for WebDAV. Sync behaviour: Rclone documentation. ↩

docs.title: Publishing in Yoda
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Publishing in Yoda page, part of VU Tools → Yoda in the A-LIFE RDM collection.

This document focuses on publishing datasets in Yoda. You can only publish a dataset after it has been archived in the Yoda Vault. By publishing, a DOI is assigned to your data package, increasing its visibility and making it findable in data catalogues such as DataCite.

  • How does the data package look once published?
  • How to publish your data in Yoda

Supporting materials: Archiving in Yoda Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-06-24 — Version: 0.1.1

✨ Did you know? VU Yoda published datasets are publicly available!

Published VU Yoda datasets are publicly accessible and searchable via DataCite Commons. Browse the full catalogue:

Explore VU published datasets on DataCite Commons

docs.title: 1. How does the data package look like once it is published?
docs.text:
When publishing a dataset, you will obtain the same type of landing page indipendently for your data classification and data accessibility you have put when completing the metadata form for archiving. The landing page is like a data cover, in which it will show all the information you have provided in the metadata form it will be visible.

But depending on what type of Data classification and Data Package Access you selected when completing the metadata form, you will see a different data content view for your landing page when you click on the DOI.

For example, when the Data Package Access is Open - freely retrievable, then the View contents blue button in the metadata page is visible underneath the Keywords of the dataset. Example how this Open published dataset will look like (obtained from DOI) once it is published with the head of the page containing the important main head metadata.

This published dataset, when accessed from the vault will then contain the Published label.

Instead, if the data is labelled as Restricted or Closed for the Data Package Access, then the content of the data is not available and the View contents is not visible on the metadata page published and only the metadata for the data package will be publicly available.

Indipendently if the access of the data content is open/closed or restricted, the main landing page of the DOI will always provide the metadata of the data package which was filled in the metadata form.

Examples of VU published datasets by data accessibility

Take a look at how a published dataset landing page looks depending on its data accessibility label:

  • Open — data and metadata are publicly accessible — DOI: 10.48338/VU01-YO96TU
  • Restricted — only metadata is publicly visible, data access requires a request — DOI: 10.48338/vu01-nwn11e
  • Closed — only metadata is publicly visible, data is not accessible — DOI: 10.48338/vu01-t4r2as

Check that your Data Classification and Data Package Access are aligned before publishing

Before publishing, it is your responsibility to verify that your Data Package Access setting matches the sensitivity of your data:

  • If your data contains sensitive or non-public data, make sure the access is set to Restricted or Closed — never Open.
  • If your data is Restricted or Closed, you must also include the appropriate custom licence file in your dataset.

For guidance on how to set these fields correctly, see the BP — Yoda — Metadata Form — specifically the Data Classification and Data Package Access sections.

docs.title: 2. How to publish your data in Yoda
docs.text:
Archiving in the Vault is required before publishing

Publishing is only possible for data packages that have already been archived in the Vault. Keep the following in mind:

  • The entire data package folder is published as a whole — you cannot publish individual files.
  • If you want to publish subfolders separately, each subfolder must be archived as its own data package first.
  • Plan your folder and archiving structure carefully before submitting to the Vault.

Not yet archived? See our Archiving in Yoda documentation for step-by-step instructions.

  1. Go to the Vault archived folder that you want to publish.
  2. Under the Actions button, click 'Submit for publication'.
  3. Select 'Submit for publication'. THis option will show when you publish the data package for the first time (e.g. first version as new version).
  4. Read the publication agreement.
  5. Click the box to agree with the statements in the agreement and click 'Confirm agreement'.
  6. Once you submit the publication, the data manager will approve the data package for publication. At this stage, a DOI with a url (landing page) will be generated containing the metadata fetched from the Yoda metadata form. This metadata set will also be registered in DataCite.

Et voilà — congratulations!

You have submitted your dataset for publication. Your dataset will shortly be made public and you will receive the DOI for your data package.

Further reading

VU Research Support Handbook — Yoda — Publishing Data

  1. The 3 images displayed in Section 2 — What to do to publish your data in Yoda were obtained from the open documentation of Utrecht University: Guide to Yoda — Publishing your data in Yoda. https://www.uu.nl/en/research/yoda/guide-to-yoda/publishing-your-data-in-yoda ↩

docs.title: 1. Requesting Storage Space in Yoda
docs.text:
To request a Yoda storage space for your project, fill in and submit the form via the VU Service Portal:

Request Yoda Space form

Important

You must be affiliated with the VU and logged in with your institutional credentials to access the form. If you are not affiliated with the VU and you are part of the project, you can still have access to the Yoda Research Space, but permissions to access the space is via invitation from the the Group data manager of the Yoda space (see Manual How to manage access to group members Yoda Research Space).

Before filling in the form, make sure you have the following information ready:

  1. Project Manager — full name of the head of the project
  2. Delegated person managing the data (if applicable)
  3. Project Budget number
  4. Estimated volume of data to be uploaded to Yoda

docs.title: 2. Metadata Fields for the Request Form
docs.text: The request form contains a number of metadata fields required to complete in order to get accepted and for the Yoda space to be created..

docs.title: 2.1 Filling in the Metadata Form
docs.text:
To help you fill in all the fields of the form in correctly, we provide a best practices guide covering each field:

Best Practices — Requesting Yoda Space

docs.title: 2.2 Submit your form
docs.text:
Once you have completed all fields, submit the form. You will receive a confirmation email within a few working days once your project space has been created.

For any questions about the form, contact the RDM Functional Application Manager: Diógenes Cruz de Arcelino — d.cruz.de.arcelino@vu.nl or use the RDM contact form to submit your questions.

docs.title: 3. Login to Yoda
docs.text: Once you receive confirmation that your Yoda project space is ready, you can log in to the Yoda Portal and start using your Yoda Research Space.

docs.title: 3.1 Go to the VU Yoda Portal
docs.text:
https://portal.yoda.vu.nl

Figure 1: Yoda VU Portal page (v.2026-06-22)

docs.title: 3.2 Provide your VU email address
docs.text:
Sign in with your VU email address.

Figure 2: Yoda SURF login page (v.2026-06-22)

docs.title: 3.3 Login with your institutional credentials
docs.text: Use your VU.nl credentials or eduID (NL).

docs.title: 3.4 Select Research
docs.text:
Select Research to access your active project space in Yoda.

Figure 1: Research Space in Yoda (v.2026-06-22)

In this space you will be able to view your project folder. The project folder maps to the name you gave when requesting the Yoda storage space.

Active storage = Research Space in Yoda

The Research Space is the active storage area in Yoda where you work with your data during the project. It is the space you have just requested access to.

What next?

You are now able to start using your Yoda Research Space — go to Step 2: Organise your Data to prepare your files before putting them in the Yoda Research Space.
